target_claim_or_section: Answer + ADV-002 / CLM-010 ('the archive is the only one that strictly cannot be bought later'; 'cannot be recreated retroactively')
challenge: The one asset the package treats as unbuyable can already be bought or downloaded. Urban Institute NCCS publishes unmodified monthly IRS EO BMF snapshots (June 2023 onward) plus legacy BMF files back to 1989; NBER and ICPSR also host historical BMF extracts. OFAC changes are published per action. Any incumbent can rebuild most of a provenance-dated archive from these public mirrors in weeks. The only gap is the entrant's own ingestion timestamps, which buyers do not value. CLM-010's limitation ('Candid or others may already hold archives') is not an edge case. It is the default, and the 'Moderate advantage if started now' verdict is not supported.
evidence: https://urbaninstitute.github.io/nccs/catalogs/catalog-bmf.html ; https://urbaninstitute.github.io/nccs/datasets/bmf/ ; https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/web/ICPSR/studies/37326/versions/V1 ; https://www.nber.org/research/data/irs-form-990-data
proposed_change: Reclassify ADV-002 as parity or near-parity, with replication of weeks from public archives. Delete 'strictly cannot be bought later' from 13 and lower CLM-010 confidence from High to Low. Before ADV-002 counts as an advantage, list exactly which fields (for example intra-month revocation timing) are absent from the NCCS, NBER and ICPSR archives.
disposition_rationale: NCCS publishes monthly BMF archive; Candid keeps history
resulting_change: ADV-002 reclassified parity; CLM-010 contradicted; 13, 24

target_claim_or_section: ADV-003, ADV-004, ADV-006 learning economies ('get cheaper and better with repetition'; replicable 12-24 months)
challenge: Learning economies favour whoever has done the most repetitions, and the entrant has done none. Foundant reports 700+ CommunitySuite community foundations, including many FIMS conversions, and has published a '500th client' milestone. Ren has moved iPhi, DonorFirst, Pinkaloo and AEF ($10.3B) books onto its platform. NPact inherited the FIMS base. Incumbents already hold the migration adapters, identity resolutions and exception rules for the main source systems. Stating 'replicable in 12-24 months' gets the direction wrong: it is the entrant that needs years to reach incumbent parity.
evidence: https://www.foundant.com/blog/foundant-technologies-hits-500th-communitysuite-client-milestone-helps-community-foundations-maximize-impact/ ; https://www.foundant.com/products/communitysuite/ ; https://www.aefonline.org/thought-leadership/ren-brings-american-endowment-foundation-fully-onto-its-technology-platform-powering-philanthropy-at-scale/ ; CLM-025 (acquisitions)
proposed_change: Add a column to competitive-advantages.csv for incumbent position today, scored ahead, equal or behind. Mark ADV-003, ADV-004 and ADV-006 as 'incumbent ahead today'. Restate the replication figure as months for the entrant to reach incumbent parity, not months for incumbents to copy the entrant.
disposition_rationale: Incumbents hold the repetition advantage
resulting_change: Incumbent-ahead noted for learning economies; 06, 13

target_claim_or_section: §1 and §3 baseline: MD-1 'Conventional manual' (183 min, $324/acct) as the comparator; CLM-037 ($493 vs $348); deterministic workflow saving $102
challenge: The model compares the entrant with a manual strawman. Mature incumbents already run deterministic workflow and automated vetting. Ren's own release lists 'automated charity vetting, rapid disbursement technology, and a digital payment system', and Ren claims 1.7-2.2M grants a year. That workload is incompatible with MD-1 touch rates. The real incumbent baseline is at least MD-3 or MD-4, so the honest AI-native gap is roughly MD-4 to MD-5: about $17-20 per account-year (CLM-011), not $183-239. This weakens the 'fundamentally lower variable cost' headline (§Answer 1) and the CLM-037 comparison.
evidence: 10 §3 table (MD-1→MD-3 $102.4; MD-4→MD-5 $17.5); https://www.aefonline.org/thought-leadership/ren-brings-american-endowment-foundation-fully-onto-its-technology-platform-powering-philanthropy-at-scale/ ; W09 grant counts
proposed_change: Make MD-3 or MD-4 the incumbent comparator, or add an 'incumbent observed' row. Restate §Answer 1 as about $20 per account-year vendor saving against an automated incumbent. Label CLM-037 as a comparison against a hypothetical manual administrator, not against Ren, Foundant or TIFIN.
disposition_rationale: Incumbents are automated; MD-1 is a strawman comparator
resulting_change: Gap restated vs MD-3 ($71) and MD-4 ($11); incumbent true mode unknown so no single figure adopted; 10

target_claim_or_section: ADV-013 published migration and exit commitments ('Differentiator until copied'; replicable 6-12 months); 16 §5 positioning #1
challenge: A published commitment is a contract clause. An incumbent can match it in the next RFP response within weeks, with no engineering (W05 already rates contract design 'trivial' at 0-6 months). Incumbents can also back the SLA with balance sheet and history: Ren took AEF from selection in July 2025 to fully live in April 2026. An entrant with no completed migration, no SOC history (CLM-040) and $0.7-1.2M of capital cannot credibly underwrite a contingent liability. Buyers will discount its promise, so the differentiation runs in reverse.
evidence: https://www.aefonline.org/thought-leadership/american-endowment-foundation-selects-ren-as-a-strategic-partner-to-expand-philanthropy-drive-innovation-and-foster-growth-in-financial-services/ ; https://www.aefonline.org/thought-leadership/ren-brings-american-endowment-foundation-fully-onto-its-technology-platform-powering-philanthropy-at-scale/ ; trackC-weakness-matrix.csv W05 '0-6'; W22 '3-6 to promise'
proposed_change: Change ADV-013 replication to 0-3 months for the promise. Add a credibility test: guarantee backing such as escrow, insurance or a bond, and a named reference migration. Reconcile the conflicting estimates of 6-12 (13), 6-12 (06 W22) and 3-6 (CSV W22).
disposition_rationale: Commitments are copyable clauses
resulting_change: ADV-013 not an advantage; 0-3 months; 13, 16

target_claim_or_section: §3 Minimum viable entry: migration assessment at contract-end windows; G1 exit criterion '≥1 authorised incumbent export rehearsed with full reconciliation'
challenge: The wedge depends on the incumbent's cooperation, and the package does not price that in. The incumbent controls the export: paid professional services, login-only access, 'as stored' formats, benchmark clauses and §2.4 third-party bans (W04, W12, W23). It also sees the renewal window first, because notice periods run 60-90 days ahead of term end, and can pre-empt with a renewal discount before an outside assessment begins. An incumbent can slow-walk or price an 'authorised export' out of the G1 timeline. 08 admits these constraints, but 16 treats the export as attainable inside 4-12 months.
evidence: trackC-weakness-matrix.csv W04, W05, W12, W23; 08-frictionless-onboarding.md line 55 (login-only access, paid exports, benchmark clauses)
proposed_change: Add incumbent export obstruction and renewal pre-emption as a named risk in 16 §6, with a probability and a fallback (for example a sponsor-run self-export only). Make the G1 exit criterion conditional on export terms reviewed in the target sponsor's signed contract before G0 spend.
disposition_rationale: Wedge depends on incumbent export cooperation
resulting_change: Named risk in 16 §7; full history conditional on contracted export; 08

target_claim_or_section: §1 Ren 'Public weakness': 'Losing iPhi community foundations (VERIFIED behaviour, W07)'; W07 classification VERIFIED-LIMITATION
challenge: 5 of 28 CFs over about 3.5 years is roughly 5% gross churn a year. Across all 57 iPhi sponsors it is 6, or about 3% a year, and national/faith is 1 of 26, about 1% a year. That is strong retention for B2B software, not a limitation. The matrix itself says 'cause UNKNOWN' and 'n/a (Ren choice)', and Ren's recent investment (AEF, advisor channels, Great Hill) points to deliberate focus away from CFs. Labelling deliberate segment exit as a 'weakness' misreads the switching record.
evidence: CLM-015; trackC-weakness-matrix.csv W07 ('cause UNKNOWN'; 'Ren choice'); 07 §1
proposed_change: Reclassify W07 as 'segment behaviour, cause unknown'. Add annualised churn figures beside the counts and drop it from Ren's 'Public weakness' column in 06 §1.
disposition_rationale: W07 is normal churn
resulting_change: Reclassified as segment behaviour with annualised rates; 06

target_claim_or_section: §1 and W09/CLM-031: 'inconsistent scale and SOC claims' (SOC 2 Type II 2025 vs Type 1 April 2026)
challenge: A SOC 2 Type 1 in April 2026 alongside a Type II in 2025 most plausibly reflects a new or expanded system scope, such as the AEF-consolidated Giving Platform going live in April 2026, which needs a Type 1 before an observation period. That is normal practice, not inconsistency. The register admits 'No SOC report inspected'. The AUM differences ($175B vs $200B; 'half' vs '>60%') line up with the AEF consolidation and different denominators. Classing this as VERIFIED-LIMITATION overstates it, and AEF's choice of Ren anyway (W09) suggests buyers read it the same way.
evidence: https://www.aefonline.org/thought-leadership/ren-brings-american-endowment-foundation-fully-onto-its-technology-platform-powering-philanthropy-at-scale/ (Apr 2026: SOC 2 Type 1; ~$200B after AEF); CLM-031 limitation
proposed_change: Downgrade W09 to 'unexplained discrepancy; scope unknown' and remove it from 06 §1 weaknesses until a scoped report or a bridge letter is inspected.
disposition_rationale: SOC difference plausibly a scope change
resulting_change: W09 downgraded to unexplained discrepancy; 06

target_claim_or_section: §3 matrix W01 (truncated history) 'Incumbent replication 6-12 months'; W02/W03/W20 '6-12 months'
challenge: The replication estimates in 06 contradict the evidence file. The CSV for W01 says '3-12 (incumbents already deliver deeper history when paid)' and gives GWCF 7 years and Arizona 26 years. The AEF 2-year default was also 'older by staff request'. Real replication time for W01 is therefore 0 months: it is a pricing and scope choice, not a capability gap. CSV W03 and W20 say 3-9, not 6-12. 06 inflates incumbent replication time against its own source register.
evidence: trackC-weakness-matrix.csv W01, W03, W20 vs 06 §3 table
proposed_change: Set W01 replication to 0 ('already delivered when contracted'). Align the W02/W03/W20 ranges to the CSV (3-18), or explain the deviation.
disposition_rationale: Replication months inconsistent with evidence
resulting_change: W01 replication 0 months; W02/W03/W20 3-6; 06

target_claim_or_section: ADV-014 single ledger 'Real; replicable 18-30 months for multi-lineage incumbents'; 06 §2 CFO row 'Ren Mixed (multi-lineage)'
challenge: The single-ledger advantage rests on W06, which is a HYPOTHESIS built on absence of evidence ('unification status unknown'). Yet 13 calls it 'Real', and 06 scores Ren's CFO position as 'Mixed' because of it. In the segment that actually switches (CFs), the integrated ledger already exists: Foundant has a 0-month replication time (W08), and 06 §6 calls it the observed winner. Ren moved AEF's entire book onto one platform in about 9 months. Calling 18-30 months 'honest' needs evidence of Ren's ledger architecture, which the package does not have.
evidence: trackC-weakness-matrix.csv W06 (HYPOTHESIS), W08 ('Already solved by Foundant... 0 months'); https://www.aefonline.org/thought-leadership/ren-brings-american-endowment-foundation-fully-onto-its-technology-platform-powering-philanthropy-at-scale/
proposed_change: Change the ADV-014 verdict to 'Unverified; parity with Foundant in CFs'. Show W06 dependency explicitly and drop 'Mixed (multi-lineage)' from 06 §2 unless ledger evidence is obtained.
disposition_rationale: Single-ledger advantage rests on hypothesis W06
resulting_change: ADV-014 marked unverified; 06 CFO row UNKNOWN; 13

target_claim_or_section: §1 Foundation Source 'Public weakness: No public SOC found (UNKNOWN W10)'
challenge: Putting 'No public SOC found' in a 'Public weakness' column breaks the package's own absence rule ('A feature missing from public pages is recorded as UNKNOWN, never as a limitation'). SOC 1 and SOC 2 reports are restricted-use and normally released under NDA, not published. Foundation Source serves TIAA and wealth-firm channels that require vendor due diligence. Absence from public search is expected and says nothing about the vendor.
evidence: 06 header 'Absence rule'; trackC-weakness-matrix.csv W10 (UNKNOWN); IBM SOC 1 note that reports are not for general public: https://www.ibm.com/products/cloud/compliance/soc-1
proposed_change: Move W10 out of the 'Public weakness' column into an 'Unknown' note for every vendor listed. Do the same for TIFIN W17 if it is shown as a weakness.
disposition_rationale: Absence rule broken
resulting_change: W10 moved to UNKNOWN; 06

target_claim_or_section: §4 'standard others adopt ... lower everyone's switching costs, which helps an entrant more than an incumbent' (network-effect option); 16 §6 HYP-013
challenge: The 'standard' option assumes incumbents would export to it. Incumbents with the largest installed bases (Ren about $200B; Foundant 700+ CFs) have no reason to adopt an entrant-authored schema, and the export terms in W04/W23 show they actively restrict data movement. Precedents such as ACATS and the Stripe SLA (CLM-022) came from a regulator or a dominant platform, not from a sub-scale entrant. Without a mandate, this standard is not a credible network-effect path.
evidence: CLM-022 (ACATS/Stripe precedents: regulator- or platform-led); trackC-weakness-matrix.csv W04, W23; https://www.foundant.com/products/communitysuite/
proposed_change: State that the standard path requires a regulator, an industry body (for example a NPT or CF coalition) or a dominant platform sponsor, and record the absence of any such sponsor as a blocking assumption. Remove the implication that it is an entrant-controllable option.
disposition_rationale: Standard path has no driver
resulting_change: Noted requirement for industry body/regulator; 13

target_claim_or_section: §3 W02/W03/W20 'Unbound can solve? Partly/Yes' vs incumbents; TIFIN velocity row
challenge: The package records TIFIN shipping an AI assistant, Chariot payments, an SEI white label, Confluence and a single-charity fund feature, roughly four or more releases in five months (CLM-032). It still gives incumbents 6-18 months to replicate queued submissions, pre-provisioned identities and in-flight registers. These are standard engineering features, not architecture. On TIFIN's observed cadence they are a one-quarter build, and incumbent AI assistance (MD-2) is acknowledged in 10 §3 as copied quickly. Replication estimates ignore the velocity evidence in the same report.
evidence: https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/02/26/3245703/0/en/TIFIN-Give-to-Power-Donor-Advised-Fund-Experience-for-Confluence-Financial-Partners.html ; https://tifin.com/news/tifin-give-partners-with-sei-to-deliver-white-labeled-donor-advised-fund-solutions-to-bank-and-trust-clients/19590/ ; https://www.investmentnews.com/fintech/tifin-give-expands-philanthropic-planning-support-with-single-charity-fund-option/259378 ; CLM-032
proposed_change: Calibrate replication months to observed incumbent release cadence: 3-6 months for feature-level items and longer only for items needing an observation period (SOC) or accumulated data. Add a 'fast follower' scenario to 16 §6.
disposition_rationale: Replication ignores incumbent release cadence
resulting_change: Feature-level replication set to 3-6 months where cited; not every row recalibrated

target_claim_or_section: §2 G1 (4-12 months) exit criterion '>=2 paying customers' sold to SEG-012/SEG-002/SEG-010
challenge: The G1 clock is inconsistent with the package's own register. market-segments.csv gives 12-24 month sales cycles for SEG-012, SEG-002 and SEG-010 (9-24), the exact segments G1 sells to. Two paying customers within 8 months of G1 start would require cycles shorter than any figure in the register, from a vendor with no references. The SEG-012 basis (announcement to go-live) measures implementation lag, not selection, so even 12-24 is probably a lower bound on time from first contact to PO.
evidence: market-segments.csv SEG-002 12-24, SEG-010 9-24, SEG-012 12-24 months; 11 §2 table; 16 §2 G1 = months 4-12
proposed_change: Re-derive the G1 duration from the register (first PO no earlier than month ~12-18 from first contact). Either extend G1 to 12-24 months and re-cost it, or change the exit criterion to signed LOIs or paid pilots rather than paying customers.
disposition_rationale: G1 timeline inconsistent with 9-24 month cycles
resulting_change: G1 extended to 6-24 months; 16

target_claim_or_section: §3 MVEP 'needs ... no SOC 1 reliance at first'
challenge: This mixes up SOC 1 and SOC 2. The wedge needs no SOC 1 report, but the migration assessment ingests donor PII and fund balances, and the evidence feed is a hosted SaaS. Any sponsor with an IT or vendor-risk function, and certainly any administrator or platform buyer, will ask for SOC 2 Type 2 or a security questionnaire plus pen test. A first Type 2 takes about 6-15 months end to end (at least 3 months of observation). Also, if the reconciliation report is used to support opening balances, the sponsor's auditor will rely on it, which is SOC 1 territory. CLM-040 already concedes a 12-24 month SOC gap, but 16 does not carry it into the wedge timeline or cost.
evidence: CLM-040 (claims.csv); 11 §3 last bullet; Drata/Scrut/Bastion SOC 2 timelines 6-15 months, >=3-month observation (vendor sources, may be optimistic); SEG-009 compliance = SOC 2 + DPA
proposed_change: Add a SOC 2 Type 1 at G0 and a Type 2 window starting in G1 as gating items, with cost (~$30-100k first year incl. tooling, ASSUMPTION) and lead time. State plainly that before Type 2 the only buyers are those willing to accept a questionnaire and a bridge letter, and size that subset.
disposition_rationale: SOC 2 and bank TPRM requirements understated
resulting_change: SOC 2 Type 1/2 and TPRM readiness in G1/G2; 14, 16

target_claim_or_section: §2/§3 vendor financial viability (G1 capital $0.7-1.2M; CLM-028 wedge never cash-positive)
challenge: Under the 2023 interagency TPRM guidance, a bank or trust buyer reviews the vendor's financial condition, usually from audited statements. The package's own models say the wedge is not cash-positive in more than 99% of ER-2 draws and needs $4-7M to reach the licensing break-even. A diligence analyst reading those numbers would flag going-concern risk and ask for source-code escrow, step-in or transition rights, and a parent guarantee or larger insurance. The 12 §4 remedy (prepaid implementation, minimum fees) also runs against buyer behaviour: buyers refuse to prepay an undercapitalised vendor because the prepayment is itself credit exposure.
evidence: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships (88 FR 37920, 2023-06-09): financial condition is a due-diligence factor (audited financials); CLM-028; 14 §1 MD-6 $4-7M; 12 §4
proposed_change: Add a 'vendor viability package' requirement (audited financials or committed funding letter, escrow, transition-assistance clause) to G1, and drop prepaid implementation as the concentration remedy for institutional buyers, or show a buyer that has accepted it.
disposition_rationale: Vendor viability is a purchase blocker
resulting_change: Partner-first entry carries balance-sheet comfort; risk listed; 07, 16

target_claim_or_section: §3 bundle 'migration assessment + charity eligibility evidence feed' as one buyable unit
challenge: Procurement would treat these as two purchases with different budget owners and contract types. The assessment is a one-time professional-services SOW from the CFO/COO project budget during re-platforming. The evidence feed is a recurring SaaS or data licence owned by grants compliance and needs a full security review, data-licence terms and an SLA. Bundling them pushes the cheap SOW through the heavier SaaS review and lengthens the cycle. There is also a conflict of interest: a sponsor in a re-platforming window is choosing a destination platform, which usually includes migration (doc 08: free migration is table stakes, CLM-021). An 'independent' assessment from a vendor that wants to become the platform will be discounted, or excluded from the RFP under independence rules.
evidence: 08 §1 'Free migration offers ... Table stakes (CLM-021)'; 08 §6 'no direct evidence'; 16 §3; CLM-016 (switches go to integrated suites)
proposed_change: Price-test the two components separately in V-2/V-8 and record budget owner and contract vehicle for each. Add a test of whether sponsors will buy an assessment from a non-destination vendor, and whether that disqualifies the vendor from the subsequent RFP.
disposition_rationale: Assessment has no buyer, no price, and no platform at G1
resulting_change: Assessment reclassified as free T0-T1 pre-sales/CAC; MVE changed to partner pilot; 08, 16

target_claim_or_section: §3 pre-signature steps 4-5 (local profiler in sponsor environment; NDA only)
challenge: Running vendor code inside the sponsor's environment is not 'NDA only'. It is a software-installation event that needs IT security review, change control and often a signed MSA, which is the same paperwork the step is meant to avoid. Sending k-suppressed aggregates also gives little protection at community-foundation scale (median 46 DAFs per SEG-002): fund-type counts and null rates for 46 funds can identify individuals. And the incumbent agreement (confidential report formats, benchmark clauses, which 08 notes but does not resolve) may forbid sharing schema or exports with a competitor before notice is given. V-4 in doc 22 says 'under NDA', but 08 §3 says real records need a DPA, so the two documents contradict each other.
evidence: 08 §3 'Not possible before signature without a data processing agreement'; 22 V-4 'One sponsor export under NDA'; 12 SEG-002 median 46 DAFs; 08 §3 constraint list (benchmark clauses)
proposed_change: Recast pre-contract work as 'paid T2 under MSA + DPA' rather than NDA. Set a minimum fund count below which no aggregates leave the sponsor. Make incumbent-contract review a precondition before any profiler runs, and fix the NDA/DPA wording in V-4.
disposition_rationale: Pre-contract work is not NDA-only; privacy duties
resulting_change: T0 no-install tier; T1 after IT approval; T2+ under MSA+DPA+WISP; 08, 16

target_claim_or_section: §1 table 'External dependence: Channel partner; hosting' (MD-6 and shared infrastructure rows)
challenge: The dependency list leaves out what a vendor-risk questionnaire asks about first: the cloud host and region, the LLM/AI provider (08 §1 relies on LLM mapping suggestions applied to sponsor data), and any data sources or subcontractors behind the evidence feed. Each is a subprocessor that must be disclosed. Donor data sent to an AI API needs DPA flow-down, no-training terms and buyer approval, and many banks require a fourth-party inventory and concentration review. The core migration engine (Transitus) is an unmerged, provisional PR (08 header), so the product being sold depends on code that does not exist on the main branch yet.
evidence: 08 header 'PR #1 not merged, provisional'; 08 §1 'LLM/ML mapping suggestions'; 14 §1 dependence column; interagency guidance on subcontractor oversight (88 FR 37920)
proposed_change: Add a subprocessor register (hosting, AI model provider, data sources, payment, email) with DPA, no-training and data-residency terms. Define an AI-off mode for buyers who ban external LLMs. Treat Transitus maturity as a G0 dependency.
disposition_rationale: Subprocessors and liability terms missing
resulting_change: Subprocessor and contract-terms registers required before G1; 14

target_claim_or_section: §1 'Liability / insurance: E&O; media rider' for charity intelligence and shared infrastructure
challenge: The insurance and liability exposure is understated. If an eligibility feed wrongly marks a charity as eligible, the sponsor may make a grant that is a taxable expenditure (IRC 4966) or an OFAC breach, and buyers will ask the vendor to indemnify that and to accept higher liability caps for data and confidentiality breaches. A migration reconciliation error that misstates opening balances is a professional-liability event. Typical buyer requirements are cyber cover of several million dollars, E&O, breach notification within 24-72 hours, audit rights and subcontractor flow-down. A $0.7-1.2M company may not be able to buy that cover at those limits, and the premiums are not in the capital estimates.
evidence: 14 §1 liability column; 16 §2 G1 capital $0.7-1.2M; SEG-009 compliance 'SOC 2, DPA'; 12 §3 eligibility service route
proposed_change: Add a contract-terms register (liability cap, indemnities, insurance limits, breach SLA, audit rights) with premiums costed into G1. Disclaim eligibility determinations explicitly (evidence, not determination) and test whether buyers accept that disclaimer in V-8.
disposition_rationale: Subprocessors and liability terms missing
resulting_change: Subprocessor and contract-terms registers required before G1; 14

target_claim_or_section: §2 'PR #88 and PR #86 used $125k per sponsor (ASSUMPTION)' and 22 G0 cost lines
challenge: The $125k CAC is untested, and the validation budget understates acquisition labour. Ten structured win/loss interviews with sponsors that switched ($5-20k) and five channel-partner conversations leading to a term sheet ($5-15k) leave nothing for senior founder time, travel, conference presence or legal review of a term sheet. A channel partner will also run its own vendor diligence on the entrant before it signs. With 12-24 month cycles, founder-led selling and a low close rate on a two-customer pipeline, fully loaded CAC for the first institutional customers is plausibly several times $125k. Section 22 also cuts acquisition cost by treating the assessment as pipeline ('value is pipeline and evidence, not margin'), so the same activity is counted as both revenue and CAC reduction.
evidence: 11 §2; 22 §1 V-1, V-6 costs; 08 §6 'value is pipeline and evidence'; SEG-001 cac_evidence 'founder-led, one long cycle per deal'
proposed_change: Build a bottom-up CAC (founder FTE-months × cycle length ÷ expected close rate, plus security and legal response costs) and run sensitivity at 2× and 4× $125k through ER-2/ER-4. Count assessment margin and CAC once, not both.
disposition_rationale: CAC untested and acquisition labour missing
resulting_change: Buyer-access line added to G0 budget; bottom-up CAC left as gap; 21, 22

target_claim_or_section: §2 G2 licensed platform via bank/trust distributor (12-36 months)
challenge: Bank and trust distribution needs the distributor's TPRM approval and then each bank's. Banks are rated 5/5 complexity in doc 11, with 6-24 month cycles and a SOC 2 Type 2 requirement that the entrant lacks for 12-24 months (CLM-040). If the SOC clock starts at G1 (month ~4-12), the first clean Type 2 arrives around months 16-28, and the bank cycle comes on top of that. A first bank go-live inside 36 months is therefore at the edge of possibility. SEI already chose TIFIN, and the distributor pool is named but unverified ('partner status unknown'). The 30k licensed-account break-even through this channel has no supporting evidence.
evidence: 11 §2 SEG-003 5/5, 6-24 months; CLM-040; 11 §3 'FIS/Fiserv wealth units; partner status unknown'; 12 SEG-003 'SEI already chose TIFIN'
proposed_change: Sequence G2 timelines as SOC Type 2 date + distributor diligence + bank cycle. Drop banks and trusts from G2 unless a named distributor reaches term-sheet stage, and model G2 on CF-software and administrator channels only.
disposition_rationale: SOC 2 and bank TPRM requirements understated
resulting_change: SOC 2 Type 1/2 and TPRM readiness in G1/G2; 14, 16

target_claim_or_section: §2 invalidation trigger 6 'slower than one customer a year'
challenge: The kill threshold is too lenient to protect capital. One customer a year at about $15-25k (V-8 bar $15k per year; V-2 bar $25k subscription) never covers G1 burn. The package already concedes that the first customer is more than 25% of revenue for years, and buyer TPRM penalises vendor concentration. The trigger should be set on revenue and reference quality (for example, at least one referenceable institutional customer with a completed security review by month X), because references are the procurement gate.
evidence: 22 §2 item 6; 22 V-2, V-8 thresholds; 12 §4 concentration; CLM-040
proposed_change: Replace the trigger with one tied to time and references: no referenceable customer that has passed a security review by month 18 means pause the thesis. Track security-questionnaire pass rate as a leading indicator.
disposition_rationale: Kill threshold too lenient
resulting_change: Time-and-reference kill rule; 16, 22

target_claim_or_section: §2 G0 exit 'or >=3 sponsors in a contract-end window willing to run a T1 assessment' (T0-T1 free per 08 §6)
challenge: A free, no-commitment T1 measures curiosity, not willingness to buy. It also contains a hidden gate: T1 needs the profiler installed in the sponsor environment (see the NDA/privacy row), so even a 'willing' sponsor may be blocked by its own IT. The G0 exit can be passed without any evidence of procurement viability.
evidence: 16 §2 G0 exit; 08 §6 'Price T0-T1 free'; 08 §3 step 4
proposed_change: Require at least one paid T2 or a signed MSA as the G0 exit, or count only sponsors whose IT has approved the profiler.
disposition_rationale: Free T1 measures curiosity
resulting_change: G0 exit is a named partner with a pilot customer; 16, 22

target_claim_or_section: Break-even assets MD-5 $1.46B base at 20 bps; MD-5 beats MD-1 ($2.11B)
challenge: breakEvenAssets = (F + n*S)/(r - v/B) leaves out capital recovery and acquisition costs. Build ($1.94M) is carried in ModeEconomics.Build but never amortised. OnetimePerSponsor/OnetimePerAcct (onboarding and migration, $36k per sponsor plus $2.67 per account) are computed but never used. CAC and the cost of capital are also missing. So "break-even" is operating contribution only, and it favours modes that own the platform over MD-1 (build 0).
evidence: Rerun via fsx on the model DLL. MD-5 at 20 bps: $1.465B base; +build amortised over 5 yrs ($388k/yr) -> $1.70B; +CAC $125k x 5 sponsors over 5 yrs and onboarding -> $1.80B; +$300k/yr SOC 1/2 audit and insurance -> $1.98B; +10% capital charge on $8.8M -> $2.51B. Build alone cuts the MD-5 vs MD-1 advantage from $0.65B to $0.41B.
proposed_change: Report fully loaded break-even beside operating break-even: amortise build, onboarding/migration and CAC over a stated life and add a capital charge. Restate CLM-013 as "$1.7-2.0B fully loaded" and the MD-1 gap accordingly.
disposition_rationale: Operating break-even omitted capital recovery
resulting_change: Added fully loaded break-even (build, CAC, onboarding amortised); 10, 15

target_claim_or_section: Capital = deepest cumulative deficit over 60 months; lowest self-sustaining capital ~$4-5M (ER-7 P50 $5.06M)
challenge: The cash model has no customer churn and no implementation/go-live lag: licence revenue starts at full run-rate on signing. It also has no ramp of migrated accounts or AUM, assumes cash on invoice with no billing in arrears or bad debt, and holds no operating reserve. A trough with zero buffer is the minimum ever-observed balance, not the amount to raise.
evidence: Python replica reproduces ER-4/5/7 base ($6.17M/$8.82M/$4.84M). Adding 10%/yr churn, a 6-month go-live lag (9 for ER-5), 3-month arrears and a 12-month account ramp gives ER-4 $8.52M, ER-5 $12.16M and ER-7 $6.86M, and none turns cash-positive within 60 months. MC share never cash-positive: ER-7 12%->60%, ER-4 17%->75%, ER-5 38%->96%. A 6-month burn reserve adds a further $0.66M (ER-7) to $1.14M (ER-5).
proposed_change: Add churn, go-live lag, account/AUM ramp, billing terms and a bad-debt line to Routes.fs. Report capital as trough plus 6-9 months reserve. Restate the self-sustaining figure as ~$6.5-8M (ER-7) until a channel partner and implementation timelines are evidenced.
disposition_rationale: Route model had no churn, lag or long horizon; censored percentiles
resulting_change: Routes: 8% churn, go-live lag, 120-month horizon, payback month; ER-2 reported as never self-funding; 15

target_claim_or_section: Monte Carlo P10/P50/P90 with independent parameters
challenge: Adverse drivers are economically correlated. Slow sales go with lower price and later revenue. Higher touch rates go with longer minutes, higher activity and higher fixed staffing. Independent draws cancel these out and compress P90 and the never-covers share. The docs say correlation "would widen the tails" but never quantify it.
evidence: Gaussian-copula rerun (adverse-direction loading on a common factor). MD-5 20 bps P90 $2.20B -> $2.82B (rho 0.3) -> $3.67B (rho 0.6). MD-5 10 bps never-covers-variable-cost 3% -> 10% -> 15%, and P90 becomes "never". Routes at rho 0.5: ER-7 P90 $6.70M -> $7.92M, never-positive 12% -> 20%; ER-4 P90 $8.57M -> $9.91M, never 17% -> 25%. P50s barely move, so the headline P50 hides the tail.
proposed_change: Run the MC with a stated correlation structure (at least rho 0.3-0.5 on a demand factor and an operating-difficulty factor) and present P90 under correlation as the capital-planning figure.
disposition_rationale: Independent draws understated tails
resulting_change: Correlated Monte Carlo (rho 0.5) for modes and routes; correlated stress scenario; 10, 15

target_claim_or_section: MD-5 vendor fixed $2.3M (PR87 lower bound + $0.1M AI governance)
challenge: The MD-6 basis itemises SOC 2/pen-test, insurance, sales and support, but the MD-5 basis itemises nothing. For a full outsourced administrator, sponsors' auditors need a SOC 1 Type II as well as SOC 2. A full administrator also needs crime/fidelity, E&O and cyber cover, segregation-of-duties staffing and a sales function. These are not visible, and running a full administrator costs only $0.7M more than licensing (MD-6). Fixed cost is flat from 1 to 10 sponsors and from $0.9B to $10B+ AUM, with no step costs. In ER-5 custodial=Y is parsed (Inputs.fs) but never used: there is no custody/trust partner fee, bond or regulatory capital.
evidence: Inputs.fs parses Custodial; no other module references it. MD-5 basis text compared with MD-6 basis text. Putting $300k/yr of audits and insurance outside the $2.3M moves 20 bps break-even $1.46B -> $1.65B. The MC 10 bps P90 ($10.9B, ~44k accounts) is served by the same $2.3M fixed.
proposed_change: Publish a line-item fixed-cost build for MD-5 (roles x loaded pay, SOC 1+2, insurance, sales, custody partner). Add step-fixed costs per sponsor and per AUM band. Either model the custodial flag or drop it.
disposition_rationale: MD-5 fixed derives from PR #87 lower bound whose $0.65M non-personnel floor includes audit, SOC 1/2 and insurance
resulting_change: No change; basis cited; SOC 1 Type II need noted in 14

target_claim_or_section: "Balance dominates"; tornado ranks avg_balance first; base $1.46B headline
challenge: The tornado leaves out fixed cost, which is the largest single driver. On its own range ($1.9-3.5M) MD-5 20 bps break-even swings $1.22B-$2.19B ($0.96B), more than balance ($0.78B). The base case also sits below the model's own P10 ($1.46B vs MC P10 $1.48B), because most ranges are skewed adverse (fixed 1.9/2.3/3.5; touch 0.6/1/2; activity 0.6/1/2.06). The same holds for registry RA-1 (base $115k vs P50 $127k) and ER-4 (base $6.17M vs P50 $6.53M).
proposed_change: Add fixed cost to the tornado and rewrite "balance dominates" as "fixed cost and balance dominate". Lead every headline with the MC P50 (and P90), and label the base case as about P5-P10 of the distribution.
disposition_rationale: Fixed cost missing from tornado
resulting_change: Added fixed_cost_mult to tornado; 10 §6

target_claim_or_section: Technology-only licensing (MD-6) breaks even at ~30k accounts at $81/account; cheapest mode for the vendor
challenge: Break-even is vendor-side only. $81 is Ren's price anchor, not a willingness-to-pay derivation. The sponsor carries 97% of event minutes, all onboarding and migration, and the change risk. The sponsor saving exists only if sponsor staff hit AI-native touch rates the vendor does not control and the sponsor removes ~14.5 FTE per 10k accounts (183 -> 26 min/acct). A 3% vendor share of event minutes for a white-label vendor (L2 support, releases, sponsor configuration) is thin, and vendors normally carry implementation.
evidence: fsx: sponsor-borne cost under MD-6 = $81 + $58 event + $20 reserved/rails vs $344 MD-1 system variable. A sponsor already paying Ren ~$81 gets $0 licence saving, so the case rests entirely on headcount reduction. Vendor share at 15% plus vendor-borne implementation ($36k + $2.67/acct = ~$63k per 10k-account sponsor, 1/yr) moves break-even 29.6k -> ~35.8k accounts (+21%).
proposed_change: Build a sponsor P&L/payback (switching cost, parallel run, contract exit, realised vs paper FTE savings, ramp to native touch rates) and derive price from it. Set the vendor support/implementation share from comparable licensing vendors, not 3%.
disposition_rationale: Sponsor-side P&L for licensing
resulting_change: System cost shows sponsor burden; full sponsor P&L deferred to V-2 price test

target_claim_or_section: Lowest defensible registry run cost ~$90-120k/yr for one sponsor (RA-1 $115k)
challenge: RA-1 zeroes RC-10, including the insurance rider, even though the registry's facts drive grant-eligibility decisions with 4966 exposure. It cuts counsel to 30 h a year and carries no on-call engineering, security, pen-test or SOC share, so it is a marginal cost resting on a platform whose fixed cost absorbs those items unstated. The 0.25 FTE "named owner" priced at $67.69/h is a fraction of a compliance officer who must exist elsewhere.
evidence: fsx Registry.cost: RA-1 $115.4k. Adding a $10k rider, 60 h counsel and 0.1 FTE on-call engineering plus $15k SOC/pen-test share gives $175.1k (+52%), and $207.6k at an 8% change rate.
proposed_change: State that RA-1 is marginal cost conditional on shared platform controls and name which fixed-cost line carries them. Give a standalone-equivalent figure (~$170-210k). Keep RC-10 conditional rather than zero until OQ-009 (TPSP) is resolved.
disposition_rationale: Registry figures are marginal cost
resulting_change: Marked marginal; standalone-equivalent ~$175k+; 05

target_claim_or_section: Charity vetting MD-5 cost $4.82/acct; registry run cost vs administration fixed cost
challenge: The event model charges vetting only $0.16 external per check (9 x 0.16 = $1.44/acct-yr). The registry run cost from doc 05 ($115k/yr for one sponsor, $1.65/grant) does not appear in events.csv, and the MD-5 fixed-cost basis does not say whether it is included. Either the registry is unfunded in the administration economics, or its omission was not stated.
evidence: At break-even (~5,860 accounts, ~53k grants) the $0.16/check external line gives ~$8.4k/yr vs RA-1 $115k. Adding $115k to MD-5 fixed moves 20 bps break-even $1.465B -> $1.534B (+$0.07B). Registry establishment ($306k) is likewise not visibly in build.
proposed_change: Add an explicit registry line (run and establishment) to MD-5/6/7 fixed or to event external cost, or cite where it sits in the $2.3M.
disposition_rationale: Registry run cost not visible in event model
resulting_change: Stated that registry (~$0.16M) is not itemised in MD fixed; adds ~$0.08B to 20 bps break-even; recorded in 20

target_claim_or_section: Shared registry ~$14-27k per sponsor at 10 sponsors
challenge: Per-sponsor cost depends on union_exponent=0.5 (10 sponsors x 20k charities -> 63k distinct charities), an untested ASSUMPTION. Mid-size sponsors with different donor bases may overlap far less.
evidence: fsx: RA-4 at 10 sponsors, union exponent 0.5 -> $27.4k per sponsor; at 0.8 (still within the stated range) -> $45.1k (+65%).
proposed_change: Run the Schedule I overlap test (ren_schedule_i_recipient_overlap.py) before quoting per-sponsor sharing economics, and quote the range at exponent 0.3-0.8.
disposition_rationale: Union exponent untested
resulting_change: Range 0.3-0.8 quoted; overlap test listed; 05, 21

target_claim_or_section: Prevention saves $33.5/acct on top of native touch rates; "no double counting"
challenge: Native touch rates are calibrated to replays of designed systems, and prevention is then applied again. EV-E10 p_native 0.09 comes from the measured 7.4-11.2% routed-to-person proxy; 40% prevention cuts it to 5.4%, below the measured range. EV-E08 p_native 0.0117 x 0.5 prevention = 0.0059, which is the "~5 reviews per 1000 grants change-driven" estimate. The native rate looks back-solved, so the "prevention value" of vetting is circular.
evidence: results.md §6: E10 prevention value $10.48/acct; removing it raises MD-5 variable cost by 0.42 bps and break-even by ~2.6% (~$0.04B). Effect is small, but the decomposition claim (prevention $33.5 vs AI $17.5) is not separable as presented.
proposed_change: State whether proxy touch rates already embed the prevention mechanisms. If they do, set prev_efficacy to 0 for E08/E10 and re-attribute the saving in the decomposition.
disposition_rationale: Prevention double counted for vetting and reconciliation
resulting_change: E08/E13 native touch rebased to pre-prevention; E10 efficacy 0.4->0.25; 09, 10

target_claim_or_section: Labour = minutes x loaded rate (FTE cost/1800 h)
challenge: Labour is costed as perfectly divisible minutes at 100% productive utilisation of 1800 h. At break-even (~5,860 accounts x 26 min = ~2,540 h = 1.4 FTE), queue coverage, PTO and segregation of duties (three-person release, independent reconciler) force whole people. Realistic touch utilisation is 60-70%.
evidence: fsx: dividing MD-5 event labour ($28.74/acct) by 0.65 utilisation moves 20 bps break-even $1.465B -> $1.522B. A minimum ops/compliance staffing floor would add more unless it is already in fixed cost, which the MD-5 basis does not show.
proposed_change: Apply a utilisation factor (0.65-0.75) to variable labour and state a minimum staffing floor per mode in fixed cost.
disposition_rationale: Labour not perfectly divisible
resulting_change: Utilisation 0.75 (0.65-1.0) applied to all labour; 09, 10

target_claim_or_section: §5 Re-vetting as verification of change; 05 §5 item 3; 17 XRI-003
challenge: The package treats the 180-day re-review as a requirement that an auditor must agree to waive. No IRS rule sets a 180-day re-review. 4966 and Rev. Proc. 2018-32 reliance turns on status at the time of the grant (TEOS/BMF/letter, unless published notice or knowledge of a change). The 180-day cycle is a sponsor policy (PR #88 / Unbound design). So the real gate is a sponsor board or policy amendment plus documented reliance, not auditor acceptance. Comparing $482k with $115k is also a straw man, because the legal floor is transaction-time status plus 4966(d)(4) checks. The '4x saving' measures a self-imposed cost, not a competitive advantage over incumbents that may not run full re-reviews at all.
evidence: Rev. Proc. 2018-32 (IRB 2018-23), which supersedes Rev. Proc. 2011-33: grantors may rely on TEOS/EO BMF for 4966 grants, except after published notice or knowledge. IRS page 'Reliance criteria for private foundations and sponsoring organizations that maintain DAFs' sets no periodic re-review requirement. No primary source for a 180-day rule is cited in 02, 04, 05 or 17.
proposed_change: Recast HYP-005/OQ-004: (a) identify where the 180-day rule comes from (Unbound policy, a sponsor policy or an auditor expectation); (b) frame it as a sponsor policy choice backed by Rev. Proc. 2018-32 reliance; (c) re-baseline CLM-005 against what incumbents actually do (transaction-time Pub 78/BMF check), not against a full re-review.
disposition_rationale: 180-day cycle is policy not law
resulting_change: Reframed in 04, 05, XRI-003; HYP-005 recast

target_claim_or_section: §5 'Every input a sponsor needs for the legal minimum ... is free and redistributable'; 02 §4
challenge: This is overstated. 4966(c)(2) exempts only 170(b)(1)(A) organizations other than 'disqualified supporting organizations'. Under 4966(d)(4), that term covers every Type III non-functionally-integrated SO, plus any Type I or Type III SO where the donor or advisor controls a supported organization. Donor control cannot be determined from IRS public files. It needs a grantee certification or donor attestation (Notice 2006-109 reliance approach), which is charity-provided or donor-provided evidence and not shareable. Other gaps public data cannot close: churches not required to seek recognition, group-exemption subordinates (Rev. Proc. 2018-32 reliance excludes subordinates not separately listed), foreign grantees needing an equivalency determination or ER, and private non-operating foundations needing ER. In 4966 terms the 'legal minimum' is not fully public-data.
evidence: IRC 4966(c)(2) and (d)(4); Notice 2006-109 §4 (certification reliance); the IRS reliance-criteria page warns that Type III NFI grants are 'subject to more restrictive rules'; the Rev. Proc. 2018-32 summary says reliance does not extend to subordinates not separately listed. 02 §4 already admits churches and subordinates need proprietary lists.
proposed_change: Add a 4966 decision tree to 04 that lists each check needing non-public evidence: SO donor-control certification, ER, equivalency determination, church and subordinate status. Route those checks to the sponsor-specific or charity-provided classes. Re-estimate the share of grants (and the exception rate in 05 and 09 E08/E10) that need non-public evidence.
disposition_rationale: Free data does not cover full determination
resulting_change: Narrowed claim to status facts; listed non-public facts; 02, 03

target_claim_or_section: §2 MD-6 'not a TPSP if no payment origination (counsel)'; 05 RC-10 and §5 item 4
challenge: This mis-frames the Nacha test. TPSP status turns on function, not on who originates. Any party that performs an ACH processing function for an Originator, ODFI or RDFI is a TPSP, and that explicitly includes creating files even if it never transmits them. A licensed platform that builds the sponsor's NACHA payment file is a TPSP almost by construction, even with the sponsor as Originator. A hybrid exception service (MD-7) that holds or releases payments, or a service that sends files to the ODFI, is more clearly a TPSP. It becomes a Third-Party Sender if the sponsor's origination agreement is with Unbound and not with the ODFI. So treating RC-10 ($44k) as conditional and 'removable' is optimistic. The OQ-009 question also asks the wrong thing: it should be 'which TPSP obligations, and who audits them', not 'whether Unbound is a TPSP'.
evidence: Nacha 'Third Parties in the ACH Network': a TPSP 'provides services related to ACH processing on behalf of another party; may or may not transmit entries directly'. Nacha consulting material and the UMACHA glossary list 'file creation' as a TPSP function. TPSPs and TPSs must complete an annual Rules Compliance Audit for the functions they perform for a DFI or TPS.
proposed_change: Assume TPSP status whenever the platform generates ACH or positive-pay files or controls release timing. Move RC-10's audit portion to 'contractually required' for MD-6, MD-7 and MD-5. Narrow OQ-009 to the Third-Party Sender question and to how audit duties are allocated.
disposition_rationale: Licensor is almost certainly a TPSP
resulting_change: TPSP audit moved to platform fixed (+$50k); 05, 14

target_claim_or_section: §6 fraud row 'Callback to aged contacts; bank-change holds ... INFERENCE (Nacha false-pretenses)'; E11/E19
challenge: The model treats fraud prevention as an optional design lever that cuts losses by 70%. Since the Nacha risk-management rules (Phase 1 on 2026-03-20; Phase 2 practically on 2026-06-22), every non-consumer Originator (the sponsor), every TPSP and every Third-Party Sender, whatever its volume, must have risk-based processes to detect entries authorized under false pretenses, reviewed at least annually. That is a mandatory control with fixed review and documentation labour per sponsor and per vendor. It is missing from the sponsor-level events E21-E23 and from the MD-6/MD-7 cost lines.
evidence: Nacha 'Risk Management Topics - Fraud Monitoring Phase 2': removes the volume threshold for non-consumer Originators/TPSPs/TPSs; effective 2026-06-19 (practically 2026-06-22); annual review required. Nacha news 2026-03-20 'New Nacha risk management rules now in effect'.
proposed_change: Add a mandatory Nacha fraud-monitoring control (design, annual review, evidence) as a fixed sponsor-year event and as a TPSP obligation in 14 §3. Recast §6's fraud lever as a compliance floor and not an ASSUMPTION-level saving.
disposition_rationale: Fraud monitoring mandatory under Nacha 2026 rules
resulting_change: Lever restated as effectiveness, not optional; 09

target_claim_or_section: §3 OFAC row 'Must remain with sponsor (sponsor is the US person making payments)'; 04 §2/§4
challenge: Two problems. (1) OFAC obligations are not only the sponsor's. Any US person, including a US software or service company that screens, clears, holds or releases payments, is barred from dealing in blocked property or facilitating prohibited transactions. Liability is strict, so a vendor that 'triages alerts' and clears a true match carries its own exposure. The table hides this. (2) The architecture does not cover the OFAC 50% rule or non-SDN programmes: entities owned 50% or more by SDNs do not appear on SLS lists, so 'free CSL/OFAC suffice' (05 RC-05) is incomplete for foreign and fiscally sponsored grantees. A third gap: OFAC recordkeeping rose from 5 to 10 years (31 CFR 501.601, IFR Sept 2024, final 2025-03-21). Screening evidence and decision replay records need a 10-year minimum retention class, which affects RC-01/RC-02 and contract terms.
evidence: 31 CFR 501.601 as amended (90 FR, 2025-03-21, final rule 2025-04864) under 21st Century Peace through Strength Act §3111; OFAC strict-liability enforcement guidelines (31 CFR part 501 App. A); OFAC 50% guidance (2014).
proposed_change: Change the OFAC row to 'sponsor accountable; the vendor has its own direct obligations as a US person'. Require a contractual allocation of screening errors. Add 50% rule and ownership screening as a gap for foreign or intermediary grantees. Set the screening and decision record retention class to at least 10 years.
disposition_rationale: Vendor has own OFAC obligations
resulting_change: 14 delegation table

target_claim_or_section: §3 MVP 'needs no custody, no payment origination, no SOC 1 reliance at first'; G1 migration assessment; 08 §3
challenge: The wedge product, a paid migration assessment that reconciles a real incumbent export, puts donor names, addresses, fund balances, grant histories, bank details and anonymity flags in a vendor's hands before any operating contract. That raises three obligations the package does not treat as gating. (a) Data protection: Unbound is a for-profit that handles nonpublic personal financial information for a financial-service provider, so the FTC Safeguards Rule (16 CFR 314, with breach notice to the FTC for 500+ consumers since 2024) and bank-affiliated sponsors' GLBA vendor oversight may apply. State comprehensive privacy laws that reach nonprofits (e.g., Colorado, Oregon, Minnesota, New Jersey, Delaware) may require processor contracts and DPIAs. (b) Incumbent contract terms: confidentiality and benchmark clauses on exports. (c) Donor-privacy notices that limit disclosure. 08 mentions these in one line, but 16 still calls the wedge low-burden. The Blackbaud enforcement precedent (SEC $3m; 49 states plus DC $49.5m; FTC order), which the repo already cites, shows the cost of getting this wrong.
evidence: 16 CFR 314 (FTC Safeguards Rule, amended 2023 with notification effective 2024); state privacy statutes with nonprofit coverage (CO CPA; OR OCPA from 2025-07-01; MN; NJ; DE); repo DAF-INDUSTRY-REPORT-2026-11.md line 767 (Blackbaud enforcement). 08 §3 says real records cannot be loaded without a DPA.
proposed_change: Make a DPA, an information-security programme (WISP), a privacy assessment and an incumbent-contract review a G1 entry criterion. Add their cost (counsel and security, plausibly $30-80k plus SOC 2 Type I) to the G1 capital line. Specify that the default assessment mode is sponsor-hosted profiling with no PII egress.
disposition_rationale: Pre-contract work is not NDA-only; privacy duties
resulting_change: T0 no-install tier; T1 after IT approval; T2+ under MSA+DPA+WISP; 08, 16

target_claim_or_section: §2 G2 distribution via bank/trust distributor; 14 §2 'Low-moderate: SOC 1/2'
challenge: Selling through a bank or trust distributor makes Unbound a bank third party under the Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships (June 2023). If the activity is critical, it can also be examined directly by federal banking agencies under the Bank Service Company Act (12 USC 1867(c)). Expect bank due diligence questionnaires, rights to audit, exit and BCP requirements, concentration-risk reviews and long procurement cycles. These are not captured by 'SOC 1/2'. The research rates regulatory exposure for MD-6 as low-moderate and does not price bank TPRM or examination readiness into ER-7 or into G2's 12-36 month timeline.
evidence: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (FRB/FDIC/OCC, 88 FR 37920, June 2023); Bank Service Company Act 12 USC 1867(c). 12 already notes '5/5 procurement' difficulty for the bank segment.
proposed_change: Add bank TPRM and examination readiness as a cost and time line for G2's bank channel (diligence, contract clauses, possibly SOC 1 Type II from day one). Raise MD-6 regulatory exposure to moderate when it is sold through banks.
disposition_rationale: SOC 2 and bank TPRM requirements understated
resulting_change: SOC 2 Type 1/2 and TPRM readiness in G1/G2; 14, 16

target_claim_or_section: §2 and §5; 16 G2 advisor/bank channels; whole package
challenge: The package does not mention the November 2023 proposed 4966 regulations (88 FR 77922, REG-142338-07), which are still pending, with a 2026-27 Priority Guidance Plan item. The parent repo's own report records this. The proposal would treat a personal investment adviser who manages both a donor's assets and the DAF as a donor-advisor, which bars compensation from the DAF under 4958. It would also tighten the definitions of 'distribution' and 'DAF'. That bears directly on the advisor-distributed and bank/trust channel economics (adviser compensation, RCF-style revenue share) that 06, 07 and 16 treat as structural facts. It also bears on 4967 and 4958 rule-engine scope. Finalization could change channel incentives (in both directions) and product requirements.
evidence: 88 FR 77922 (2023-11-14; FR doc 2023-24982); docket IRS-2023-0053 (249 submissions per repo); 2026-2027 Priority Guidance Plan item on §§4966/6033; repo DAF-INDUSTRY-REPORT-2026-11.md line 767.
proposed_change: Add a regulatory-scenario row to 16 §6 ('What would make this wrong'): final 4966 regs adopt the adviser-as-donor-advisor rule. Model its effect on the channel thesis (CLM-017) and add 4958 and adviser-fee rules to the rule-engine scope.
disposition_rationale: Pending 4966 proposed regulations omitted
resulting_change: Added to 14 and 16 §7

target_claim_or_section: §2 MD-5 full-service administrator; MD-7 exception service; state exposure absent
challenge: The package does not assess state charity regulation. An administrator that 'holds and releases charitable money' or receives and controls contributions for compensation may fall within state definitions of commercial fundraiser, fundraising counsel or professional solicitor. California's 'commercial fundraiser for charitable purposes' (Gov. Code 12599) covers persons who receive or control charitable funds for compensation. That brings registration, bonding, contracts filed with the AG and annual reporting across many states. Separately, state AG registry status (e.g., CA AG Registry 'delinquent' or 'suspended', which bars soliciting or disbursing) may be eligibility-relevant for some sponsor policies but is classed as an 'optional' paid input (RC-05). Uncashed grant checks (E12) are also unclaimed property in most states, a reporting duty the model does not include.
evidence: Cal. Gov. Code 12599 (commercial fundraiser definition); CA AG Registry of Charities and Fundraisers (delinquency consequences, 11 CCR 999.9.x); state unclaimed property acts (RUUPA). No mention of 'solicitation', 'fundraiser' or 'unclaimed' in the package (grep).
proposed_change: Add a state-law workstream: a counsel opinion on fundraiser and fundraising-counsel status for MD-5 and MD-7 in the top 10 states; whether state registry delinquency belongs in default eligibility rules; and an unclaimed-property event in 09 (E12 and close).
disposition_rationale: State fundraiser law not assessed
resulting_change: Added to 14 with counsel item

target_claim_or_section: §2 'Shared vetting evidence ... screening result at time t' and 'Unresolved conflict ... Shareable (as a flag)'; 05 RA-4; 14 'media rider if publishing'
challenge: Sharing screening results and conflict flags across sponsors is a legal question, not only a licensing one. A false sanctions or 'unresolved conflict' flag on a charity that is redistributed to many sponsors creates defamation and tortious-interference exposure. Screening results about individual officers are personal data, so cross-sponsor reuse needs a lawful basis under state privacy law and processor terms. Coordinated shared exclusion signals among competing sponsors raise antitrust and group-boycott questions, which 14 flags only for the federated model. The package treats this as an insurance rider (RC-10) and 'OQ-010 contractual terms'.
evidence: 04 §2 table (screening result and conflict shareable); 14 §2 federated row ('antitrust and data-sharing terms (counsel)'); 05 RC-10 'rider only if registry facts are published'.
proposed_change: Share only source-attributed facts. Never share derived flags or screening dispositions; each sponsor's match decision stays sponsor-specific. Strip individual-officer screening results from the shared layer. Add a counsel question on defamation, privacy and antitrust for RA-4, separate from OQ-010.
disposition_rationale: Shared flags carry legal and tenancy risk
resulting_change: Screening sponsor-scoped; no promotion from confidential inputs; snapshot pinning; licensed class; 04

target_claim_or_section: §1 AI factor 0.6 on minutes per touch; E10 grant approval 12.25 min AI-native; 04 §6
challenge: 04 rightly keeps AI advisory, but 09 books the saving anyway: humans review AI dossiers 40% faster. The package does not test whether a review that fast is a meaningful human decision. It ignores automation bias, documentation of reasoning for auditors, and model-risk controls (validation, change management, prompt and version logging tied to the decision record). If an examiner or auditor finds 'rubber-stamp' review of AI-prepared 4966/4967 determinations, the claimed reduction in human minutes for E10 and E08 is the first thing to go. Where donor-facing AI is used for account or fraud holds, state AI laws (e.g., the Colorado AI Act on consequential financial-service decisions, delayed to mid-2026) may also add duties.
evidence: 09 §1 (AI factor 0.6 is ASSUMPTION; HYP-008); 04 §2 AI-generated assessment row; Colorado SB24-205 as delayed by SB25B-004.
proposed_change: Add a model-risk and human-review-quality control event (sampling of AI-assisted decisions; reviewer override rates) with its own minutes. Make HYP-008 conditional on an auditor accepting the AI-assisted review evidence.
disposition_rationale: AI-assisted review quality
resulting_change: AI oversight cost added; review-quality sampling event deferred

target_claim_or_section: ADV-002 / CLM-010: temporal archive of IRS releases 'cannot be recreated retroactively'; 'the only one that strictly cannot be bought later'
challenge: The BMF half of the archive already exists outside Unbound. The Urban Institute's NCCS publishes raw, unmodified monthly IRS BMF releases (raw/bmf/YYYY-MM-BMF.csv), with a transformed series from 2023-06 to 2026-07 and harmonized vintages back to 1989, though the series has gaps. The package's own change-rate evidence (charity-network 06 section 2.1) was computed from this 'NCCS mirror of IRS monthly files'. Candid says it pings the IRS every 20 minutes, downloads BMF, Pub 78 and revocation files on change, and keeps revocation and reinstatement history on the record. ICPSR also holds BMF extracts. The auto-revocation file is itself cumulative, with effective dates, posting dates and reinstatements. That leaves Pub 78 snapshots and fine-grained provenance as the only parts that are plausibly scarce.
evidence: urbaninstitute.github.io/nccs/catalogs/catalog-bmf.html (raw monthly archive; legacy 1989-2022); urbaninstitute.github.io/nccs/datasets/pub78 (no Pub 78 history); developer.candid.org/reference/faqs-charity-check ('ping the IRS website every 20 minutes'; revocation and reinstatement kept 'for research purposes'); charity-network 06 s2.1 [REG-012] cites the NCCS mirror. Wayback CDX was blocked from this session (UNVERIFIED).
proposed_change: Downgrade ADV-002 from 'moderate advantage' to 'hygiene / parity for BMF; possible narrow edge only for Pub 78 snapshots plus hash-level provenance'. Change CLM-010 to state that NCCS, Candid and ICPSR already hold BMF history. Add an evidence-gap item to check Internet Archive and GivingTuesday holdings of Pub 78 and the revocation files.
disposition_rationale: NCCS publishes monthly BMF archive; Candid keeps history
resulting_change: ADV-002 reclassified parity; CLM-010 contradicted; 13, 24

target_claim_or_section: RP-07 evidence_expiry_share base 0.10 (5-20%) vs 04 s4 expiry periods (bank 24 months; website 12 months)
challenge: The parameter contradicts the architecture's own expiry rules. If every charity in use has a bank letter that expires every 24 months and a website check that expires every 12 months, expiry events run at about 150% of charities a year, not 10%. At 20k charities and 5 minutes each, that is about 2,500 hours against about 167 hours. The gap is about $155k a year at $67.69 an hour, which is more than the whole RA-1 run cost. Bank re-verification is also rarely a 5-minute task, because it needs contact with the charity or a vendor.
evidence: 04 s4: 'bank verification 24 months; website check 12 months'; registry-parameters.csv RP-07 0.1 ASSUMPTION; RP-08 5 min ASSUMPTION; RP-14 $67.69/h
proposed_change: Derive RP-07 from the expiry table: sum over evidence types of the share of charities holding the evidence divided by the validity in years. Separate bank re-verification, priced as a vendor fee or charity outreach, from website checks. Rerun RA-0 to RA-7 and restate the $90-120k floor.
disposition_rationale: Expiry rate inconsistent; name-match alerts missing
resulting_change: Expiry 0.5/charity-year; alert rate 1%/charity-year at 10 min; 05

target_claim_or_section: RP-02 4% eligibility-relevant change rate (basis: 405 adverse-candidate BMF changes per month plus 'monitoring 4% status events')
challenge: The 4% counts IRS status events, but the package adds several monitoring feeds whose alerts are not in that number. These are the full trade.gov CSL (26,339 rows), the UK, UN and EU lists, SAM exclusions, FAC going-concern and material-weakness flags, the CA AG 'may not operate' list, and state corporate dissolution. Name-only screening of organisation names against roughly 26k export-control and sanctions rows produces false positives at every delta. OFAC alone updates 110-130 days a year, and charity names such as 'Al-...', 'Relief', 'Foundation for ...' or 'Islamic ...' match often. Those dispositions are exception work. The 4% also comes from one month of BMF diffs (06 rates it Medium for annualisation) and the August revocation batch, so peak load is far above the mean.
evidence: 02 s1-2 (CSL, SAM, FAC added as monitoring signals); charity-network 06 s2.1-2.2 (one month; about 70% of revocations post in August; OFAC update days); registry-parameters RP-02 basis
proposed_change: Split RP-02 into (a) IRS status events, (b) screening alerts from name matching and (c) FAC, SAM and state flags. Measure (b) by screening a real 20k charity list against the CSL and SDN with the intended matcher. Model the August revocation peak for staffing, not just the annual mean.
disposition_rationale: Expiry rate inconsistent; name-match alerts missing
resulting_change: Expiry 0.5/charity-year; alert rate 1%/charity-year at 10 min; 05

target_claim_or_section: RP-03 45-minute mean exception (30-60) with 20-30% deterministic auto-resolution
challenge: The basis is an assumption carried over from a sibling package ('charity-network ECO C0 45 min'), not a measurement. In practice the exception mix has a heavy tail. Catholic parishes need an OCD page plus a cover page. Other church and subordinate cases need the central organisation to confirm. Successor and merger cases need documents and sponsor approval. Foreign equivalency, Type III supporting organisations, DBA and fiscal-sponsored project binding, and payment-destination mismatches also need outreach. Many of these involve waiting on the charity for days and several contacts, so hands-on time often runs to hours. A 45-minute mean is plausible for screening false positives and poor for the rest. Section 5 then makes 45 minutes a condition the operator 'must demonstrate', which is circular, because the cost conclusion already rests on it.
evidence: registry-parameters RP-03 basis; 02 s3 identity table; trackA-notes s2.7 (OCD cover-page requirement for USCCB GEN 0928); 05 s5 item 2
proposed_change: Model exceptions by class, each with its own minutes and elapsed-days distribution, using a lognormal or triangular with a fat right tail. Report the cost at P90 handling time. Label the 45-minute mean UNVERIFIED until a timed sample of real exceptions exists.
disposition_rationale: Exception minutes borrowed, heavy-tailed
resulting_change: Flagged as circular; class-based exception model deferred to V-3/V-7

target_claim_or_section: 'Every input a sponsor needs for the legal minimum ... is free and redistributable'; 'Yes for determinations' (03 s5; 02 s4)
challenge: This is true for IRS status and sanctions, but not for the full DAF determination. Section 170(c)(1) governmental grantees (public school districts, public universities, municipalities, tribal governments) are eligible but appear in neither Pub 78 nor the BMF. Non-applicant churches are absent too. Section 4966 and 4967 rules on Type I and III supporting organisations, and the Type III functionally-integrated versus non-functionally-integrated split, turn on control by donors or disqualified persons. Public data cannot show that, so a certification from the charity is needed. Organisations recognised too recently to appear in Pub 78 or the BMF are missing as well (Candid's 'advanced status' comes from determination letters charities upload). Foreign grantees need equivalency or expenditure responsibility. Free data supports status determinations, not eligibility determinations.
evidence: developer.candid.org FAQ ('advanced status' from determination letters, not in the API); Candid field docs (FED/government deductibility type; church messages); 02 s3 (foreign equivalency left to the sponsor); IRC 4966(d)(4) and 4967 (statutory)
proposed_change: Restate the claim as 'free data suffices for IRS status, revocation, sanctions and exclusion facts'. Add governmental units, new determinations and supporting-organisation control certifications as named coverage holes with an evidence class (charity-provided or certified). Add their exception volume to RP-05.
disposition_rationale: Free data does not cover full determination
resulting_change: Narrowed claim to status facts; listed non-public facts; 02, 03

target_claim_or_section: s6: charity intelligence could be a product as an 'eligibility evidence service' (status, screening and change history via API)
challenge: The price ceiling is already low. Candid Charity Check starts at $2,750 a year. Its 40+ fields already combine BMF, Pub 78, Internal Revenue Bulletin, auto-revocation, OFAC SDN and 501(p) status, a subordinate-inheritance indicator, church messages and a California AG and FTB endpoint, with a bulk tier of 25 organisations per call and timestamped PDF evidence. Pactman Nonprofit Check Plus is free up to 200 checks a month. Treasury Do Not Pay offers federal agencies Pub 78 continuous monitoring at no cost. The differentiators left are change history and event push, and Candid's lack of a monitoring endpoint can be closed cheaply. The 'incumbent paid market' line understates this. On the evidence, the market is a commodity sold at a few thousand dollars a year.
evidence: developer.candid.org/llms.txt (Charity Check, Bulk, PDF and California endpoints); developer.candid.org/reference/interpret-charity-check-data-fields (OFAC Status, Pub78 Indicator 2 = subordinate, church messages); search results for Candid pricing 'starting at $2,750'; Pactman Nonprofit Check Plus listing (free 200/month); fiscal.treasury.gov irs-teos-qrc.pdf (Do Not Pay continuous monitoring)
proposed_change: Add a competitor price table for Candid, Pactman, Do Not Pay and Every.org/OrgHunter. Test HYP-007 against a willingness-to-pay ceiling of about $3-10k a year per sponsor for status and screening. Treat ER-1 as unattractive unless replayable decision evidence with audit acceptance is the thing being sold.
disposition_rationale: Candid $2,750 sets a commodity price ceiling
resulting_change: Charity intelligence reclassified as component; 02, 16

target_claim_or_section: RA-5 commercial licence $60k base ($25-150k; RP-12 'price not published, UNKNOWN')
challenge: The package's own source register records Candid APIs 'From $2,750/yr (vendor list price per repo)', and Charity Check pricing is published as starting at $2,750. That is an order of magnitude below the RA-5 base, so the conclusion that commercial enrichment is 'the most expensive single-sponsor option' is driven by an assumption that contradicts the register. Enterprise or bulk redistribution licences may cost more, but the use the model assumes (enriching one sponsor's own decisions) is the low-tier use case.
evidence: data/registers/charity-data-sources.csv row CANDID ('From $2,750/yr'); registry-parameters RP-12; registry-alternatives RA-5 commercial_licence_usd 60000
proposed_change: Set the RP-12 low value at about $2.75k and the base from a tiered quote assumption, then rerun RA-5. If RA-5 then becomes competitive with RA-1, note that it buys Candid's DBA, alias and advanced-status data, which addresses the identity holes in 02 s3.
disposition_rationale: Commercial licence mis-anchored
resulting_change: RP-12 anchored to Candid $2,750 list price; 05

target_claim_or_section: Identity table (02 s3): 'EIN reuse and mergers - BMF silent removal on revocation; no tombstone'; group subordinates as a roster problem; DBA via alias table
challenge: This misdescribes the hard identity problems. The IRS does not reassign EINs, so the real failures run the other way. Conversions, mergers and reincorporations produce new EINs for the 'same' charity. Some EINs are shared by many operating units: fiscal-sponsored projects (the package counts 20,566), chapters, and subordinates who list the central organisation's EIN. Revocations are not tombstone-less either, because the cumulative auto-revocation file is the tombstone. The dominant DAF identity task is mapping a donor's free-text name or DBA to an EIN. Pub 78 carries no DBAs, and the BMF truncates names, so this depends on alias data that only self-reported aggregators such as Candid hold. The 800-hour entity-resolution establishment budget and 'candidate links, never auto-merge' do not size this work.
evidence: 02 s3; charity-network 06 s2.2 (revocation file with reinstatement dates = history); Treasury TEOS QRC ('If an organization uses a doing business as (DBA) name, that name will not be listed in the PUB 78 Data'); 02 s1 (Fiscal Sponsor Directory 20,566 projects)
proposed_change: Rewrite the identity table around (1) donor name or DBA to EIN, (2) one EIN for many units (fiscal sponsor, chapter, subordinate), (3) one charity across many EINs (succession). Measure the hit rate of name-to-EIN matching on a sample of real donor grant requests before fixing the RP-05 exception rate.
disposition_rationale: EIN reuse framing wrong
resulting_change: Identity table rewritten; 02

target_claim_or_section: '0 of 237,380 c3 subordinates appear in Pub 78'; churches and subordinates are a 'structural hole that no public source fills'; 'only proprietary OCD and ECFA lists exist'
challenge: This overstates the problem. The 237k subordinates are in the BMF with a group exemption number and affiliation codes, and the central organisation's annual roster submission keeps that listing current. Candid's Pub78 Indicator = 2 shows a vendor automating subordinate eligibility from the central organisation's record. The genuine hole is narrower: non-applicant churches, plus large groups like USCCB GEN 0928 whose subordinates are not individually listed. The case also cuts the other way for the package. If subordinate status can be largely automated from the BMF, it does not justify the exception-labour assumptions. If it cannot, the 4% and 45-minute figures undercount it. The package uses it both ways (a structural hole in 02, absent from RP-02 and RP-03).
evidence: developer.candid.org/reference/interpret-charity-check-data-fields (Pub78 Indicator 2 'subordinate ... inherits its data from the central organization'; GROUP deductibility); charity-network 06 field counts (GROUP and AFFILIATION changes); trackA-notes s2.7
proposed_change: Quantify the BMF-listed subordinates (automatable via GEN) separately from unlisted church and Catholic units (evidence workflow). Estimate the share of DAF grant volume going to each, for example from a sample of donor-advised fund grant reports, and feed the unlisted share into the exception model.
disposition_rationale: Subordinates are listed in BMF via GEN
resulting_change: Corrected; 02

target_claim_or_section: Licensing classes: state data treated as public domain or 'Yes' independent; shared registry may hold 'public-domain and open-licensed facts' only
challenge: 17 USC 105 covers federal works only. State AG registries (CA AG 'may not operate', NY), state corporate registries other than Colorado's explicit public-domain dedication, and NASCO material have state-specific terms, copyright claims or paid-bulk contracts (GA $1,000, IN $9.5k+). The package already marks several of these UNKNOWN, yet 02 counts the CA list as 'supports automation' and RA-4 assumes a shared layer. The shared registry's actual dependency is also undisclosed: the package's own change-rate measurement used the NCCS mirror, whose licence was not recorded.
evidence: 03 s1 table (no row for CA AG or NY AG terms); 02 s1 (CA list 'supports automation'); charity-network 06 [REG-012] NCCS mirror; NCCS catalog page shows no licence text
proposed_change: Add a licence row per state source actually planned, at minimum CA AG and NY AG. Record the NCCS licence or ingest directly from the IRS for any production replay. Keep state facts out of the shared layer until terms are confirmed by counsel (OQ-007).
disposition_rationale: State sources not public domain
resulting_change: Licence note per state source; 03

target_claim_or_section: EV-E08, EV-E10, EV-E13 native touch rates combined with prevention efficacy
challenge: Prevention is applied multiplicatively on top of native touch rates that were themselves calibrated to the prevented state. EV-E08 p_native 0.0117 is sourced from the 'change-driven vetting central estimate ~5 per 1000' and then the prevention 'change-driven continuous monitoring' (0.5) halves it again; EV-E13 p_native 0.01 assumes the native ledger and then 'single ledger with continuous reconciliation' (0.5) halves it again; EV-E10 0.09 comes from the PR #88 replay proxy, which already routed lines through policy rules, and is cut a further 40% by 'pre-validated policy rules'. The same mechanism is credited twice.
evidence: Events.fs touchProb: raw * (1 - PrevEfficacy*prevention_scale); 09 table E08 MD-5 0.79 min = 9 x 0.0117 x 0.5 x 15; events.csv basis columns for E08/E10/E13
proposed_change: For each event, either restate p_native as the pre-prevention rate or set prev_efficacy to 0 where the basis already embeds the mechanism. Rerun MD-4/MD-5 and the 10 §3 decomposition; the prevention line ($33.5) and the MD-5 minutes (26) should both move.
disposition_rationale: Prevention double counted for vetting and reconciliation
resulting_change: E08/E13 native touch rebased to pre-prevention; E10 efficacy 0.4->0.25; 09, 10

target_claim_or_section: MD-3..MD-5 build $1.1-2.4M (base $1.94M); platform run cost ~$0.7M/yr
challenge: At rate_engineering $118/h, $1.94M buys about 16.4k hours, or about 9 engineer-years. The implied scope is a multi-tenant bitemporal ledger with three isolation profiles, payment origination with positive pay and dual release, custodian feeds, identity, OFAC screening, a nine-class charity registry with three time axes, the Transitus migration engine, donor and advisor portals, statements and acknowledgments, and a continuous-control-monitoring system ready for SOC 1 and SOC 2. Comparable fintech cores (ledger plus payments plus compliance) usually take 20-40 engineer-years before a first audited go-live. The $0.7M run budget is about 3.3 engineering FTE, which cannot staff a sustainable 24x7 on-call rotation for payment release while also absorbing custodian, bank, Nacha and IRS format changes.
evidence: parameters.csv PAR-006 $118/h; enterprise-modes.csv MD-3..MD-5 basis 'MSP build $1.1-2.4M'; Unbound TENANT-AWARE-PERSISTENCE-DESIGN (3 profiles, engine not selected, ADR-001..009 open); CONTINUOUS-CONTROL-MONITORING spec (20+ object types)
proposed_change: Cost the build bottom-up against the component list (ledger, payments, tenancy, registry, migration, portals, control monitoring, SOC readiness) with explicit FTE-years. Show a high case of $5-8M and run cost of $1.2-1.8M with a 5-6 person on-call floor. Rerun break-even and 15 capital tables, and state that the agent-assisted multiplier (RC-AN-015) is the only thing supporting the low end.
disposition_rationale: Build budget may be low for implied scope
resulting_change: Build high widened to $3.6M; bottom-up build costing left to Unbound (PR #87 owns the derivation)

target_claim_or_section: MD-6/MD-7 'same system cost, differs only in who carries it'
challenge: The model applies vendor_event_share to the whole event cost and uses identical native touch rates, the 0.6 AI factor and the same hourly rates for sponsor staff. In practice, sponsor staff at a 5-sponsor scale handle a few exceptions a week, so they cannot keep specialist proficiency.
