They also face indivisible minimum staffing (a fraction of a compliance FTE cannot be hired), need integration work with their own GL, bank and custodian, and carry their own vendor-management and SOC-report review overhead. In addition, the share is applied to AI inference, prevention cost and expected failure loss, so in MD-6 the vendor bears only 3% of the AI compute it runs on its own platform.
evidence: Enterprise.fs: VendorVariablePerAcct = eventPerAcct * share + infra; SystemVariablePerAcct identical across MD-5/6/7; enterprise-modes.csv MD-6 vendor_event_share 0.03
proposed_change: Add a sponsor efficiency penalty (1.3-2.0x minutes per touch), a minimum sponsor staffing floor per sponsor (e.g. 0.5-1 FTE), and one-time integration cost per sponsor. Keep AI and platform-run costs with the vendor regardless of share. Restate the MD-6 break-even ($0.85B) and the 'same system cost' claim.
disposition_rationale: Licensing assumed equally efficient sponsor staff; vendor escaped AI compute
resulting_change: Sponsor efficiency x1.4; vendor bears AI compute in licensing; 10, 14

target_claim_or_section: ADV-014 single ledger 'removes reconciliation'; EV-E13 prevention 0.5
challenge: The DAF has no single ledger. Assets sit at a custodian, cash at a bank, and the sponsor's audited books in its own GL. A unified operational ledger removes internal re-keying, but breaks caused by custodian pricing, corporate actions, settlement timing, ACH returns, check float and bank fees remain, and those external breaks are the main reconciliation workload. The ledger itself is also commoditised: off-the-shelf double-entry ledgers and ledger APIs let any incumbent or entrant stand one up in months, not 18-30.
evidence: events.csv EV-E13 basis 'breaks 1% of transactions' (external); 14 §3 sponsor retains financial statements and audit; ADV-014 'replicable in 18-30 months'
proposed_change: Reclassify ADV-014 as an ordinary capability. Split EV-E13 into internal and external breaks and apply prevention only to internal breaks. Keep three-way reconciliation (ledger-custodian-bank) and the sponsor GL tie-out as irreducible human work in every mode.
disposition_rationale: Single ledger does not remove external reconciliation
resulting_change: ADV-014 restated; prevention applies to internal breaks; 10, 13

target_claim_or_section: Prevention levers EV-E04 (notification-first intent / virtual accounts), EV-E03, EV-E11 positive pay, EV-E06 custodian feeds
challenge: The prevention efficacies depend on third parties that the vendor does not control. Virtual accounts and positive pay need a bank product (with fees and onboarding). Fund references on securities transfers depend on the delivering broker populating DTC/ACATS fields, which they often truncate or omit. Custodian feeds need contracts and approval from each custodian. Payment origination needs an ODFI relationship and, if the vendor acts as a third-party sender, an annual Nacha audit and bank due diligence (often 6-12 months). Doc 09 calls these a 'commercial dependency' but applies them at full efficacy in the base case.
evidence: 09 §6 last paragraph; parameters.csv PAR-017 prevention_scale base=high=1.0; 14 §3 Nacha row 'requires counsel (OQ-009)'
proposed_change: Set the base prevention_scale to 0.5 or lower until a bank or custodian partner is signed. Add a dependency register entry (ODFI, custodians, virtual-account bank, check/lockbox vendor, identity vendor, OFAC list provider) with lead time and fee to the capital plan, and add partner lead time to time-to-revenue (15-18 months looks optimistic).
disposition_rationale: Prevention depends on third parties
resulting_change: Base prevention scale 0.5 until partners signed; 09, 10

target_claim_or_section: fail_mult_automated base 0.8; expected-value failure cost
challenge: Failures are modelled as independent per-event probabilities with a reduction for automation in the base case. In automated finance systems the dominant risk is correlated: one bad rule version, a mis-parsed IRS release, a duplicate payment file or a bad shared-registry merge hits thousands of transactions at once. An expected-value model with independent failures structurally understates tail loss, and the base case presumes the benefit (0.8) that the high case says could reverse (1.2).
evidence: PAR-009 range 0.5/0.8/1.2; Events.fs failP = FailProb * failMult; 13 §3 notes correlated error but the model does not
proposed_change: Set base fail_mult_automated to 1.0. Add a batch or systemic failure scenario (e.g. 1 in 5 years, affecting a full payment run) to the Monte Carlo, priced with recovery, counsel and reputational cost. Require release controls (rule-version canarying, payment-file hash and duplicate checks) as fixed cost.
disposition_rationale: No evidence automation lowers failure rates
resulting_change: fail_mult_automated base 1.0 (0.7-1.5); systemic failures recorded as risk

target_claim_or_section: Shared registry with 'registry steward' confirming inferred relationships into shared decisions
challenge: The shared layer leaks across tenants and creates correlated failure. (a) When a steward promotes an identity link to shared status, the promotion is often based on one sponsor's confidential confirmation or charity-provided documents, so sponsor-derived evidence moves into the shared layer. (b) Refresh triggers and query logs show which charities a sponsor's donors are granting to. (c) One bad shared fact reaches every tenant's payment-release gate at once. (d) Unbound's tenancy design includes a dedicated-infrastructure profile that cannot consume a live shared store without a governed cross-boundary feed, which 04 does not specify. The steward also becomes a SOC 1 service organisation (13 §3), which needs its own controls and fixed cost.
evidence: 04 §2 'Inferred relationship ... steward confirmation turns it into a sponsor or shared decision'; TENANT-AWARE-PERSISTENCE-DESIGN lines 59-60 and 122-123; 13 §3
proposed_change: Forbid promotion of any link to shared status from sponsor-confidential inputs. Have each tenant pin a registry snapshot version and require explicit acceptance of eligibility-relevant deltas (per-tenant circuit breaker). Specify the cross-boundary feed for profile C. Cost the steward function and its SOC 1 Type II report in fixed cost.
disposition_rationale: Shared flags carry legal and tenancy risk
resulting_change: Screening sponsor-scoped; no promotion from confidential inputs; snapshot pinning; licensed class; 04

target_claim_or_section: Nine evidence classes + three time axes as implementable and auditable
challenge: The classes overlap: a 'screening result at time t' (shared vetting evidence) is a derived computation over an authoritative list and a sponsor-specific matching threshold, so it is not sponsor-neutral. Publication time is not reliably recoverable for IRS bulk files, which carry release dates, not per-record publication. Bank-account verification, the highest-loss evidence, is in practice supplied by third-party validation vendors whose licences usually forbid reuse across customers, and the model has no class for it. Auditability requires deterministic replay of decision rules, matcher versions and list versions, and 04 does not specify rule-version provenance or retention cost.
evidence: 04 §2 table rows 'Shared vetting evidence' and 'Charity-provided information'; §3 publication time; events.csv EV-E08 fail_loss $500 and EV-E19 fraud $20k
proposed_change: Add a 'licensed third-party verification' class with per-licence sharing flags. Make screening results sponsor-scoped (shared inputs, per-sponsor outputs). Define publication time as the source release identifier where no per-record time exists. Add rule and matcher version provenance to the decision record, and run an auditor walkthrough before XRI-002 is promoted.
disposition_rationale: Shared flags carry legal and tenancy risk
resulting_change: Screening sponsor-scoped; no promotion from confidential inputs; snapshot pinning; licensed class; 04

target_claim_or_section: Infrastructure $25/account-year owned (range $15-45)
challenge: Per-account infrastructure ignores per-tenant fixed floors. Unbound requires separate-schema, separate-database and dedicated-infrastructure profiles, each with per-tenant backups, KMS keys, logs, indexes, queues and DR testing. A dedicated HA database, DR replica, logging and security tooling cost tens of thousands of dollars a year per tenant whatever the account count. With 5 sponsors and 10k accounts, two dedicated-profile tenants alone could exceed the modelled $250k infrastructure line. Unbound's own ADR-009 leaves tier economics open.
evidence: TENANT-AWARE-PERSISTENCE-DESIGN UNB-TEC-STRATA-002, lines 123 and 160 (ADR-009); PAR-011 'SPN placeholder'
proposed_change: Model infrastructure as per-tenant fixed by isolation profile plus per-account variable. Price profile C as a pass-through surcharge, and rerun break-even with the 5-sponsor mix.
disposition_rationale: Per-tenant infrastructure floors
resulting_change: Recorded; not modelled

target_claim_or_section: EV-E03 contribution posting p_native 0.03 across cash ACH check securities; EV-E01 0.15; EV-E10 9%
challenge: These touch rates are assumptions or replay proxies, not production measurements (10 §6 admits this). Checks need lockbox or remote-deposit capture with image exceptions. Securities gifts need lot and cost-basis capture, and valuation on the gift date under the mean-of-high-low rule. A 3% blended touch rate (before prevention, then a further -30%) is implausible for a book where checks and securities are 60% of contributions by count (1.0+0.5+1.0 weighting). The tornado shows the native touch multiplier is a top-4 driver.
evidence: events.csv EV-E03 basis 'weighted ACT-A02..A04 frequencies (1.0+0.5+1.0)'; 10 §5 tornado; 10 §6
proposed_change: Split EV-E03 by channel (ACH/card, check, securities) with separate native touch rates (e.g. 1-2%, 10-20%, 20-40%). Widen touch_mult_native in the Monte Carlo to 0.5-3x, and show MD-5 break-even with measured-proxy-free inputs.
disposition_rationale: Contribution channels need separate touch rates
resulting_change: Recorded; touch range covers; split deferred to measurement

target_claim_or_section: Technology licensor: 'not a TPSP if no payment origination'; low-moderate regulatory exposure
challenge: If the licensed platform generates the ACH or positive-pay files, holds release workflows or stores payee bank details, banks and auditors will treat the vendor as in scope as a SOC 1 service organisation and probably as a third-party service provider under Nacha. Even when the sponsor is the Originator, the vendor will face ODFI due diligence, data-security rules for account numbers, and contract liability for payment errors. The 'low-moderate' rating and the E&O and cyber-only insurance understate this, and MD-7's exception desk acting on payments compounds it.
evidence: 14 §2 Technology licensor row; 14 §3 Nacha row 'requires counsel (OQ-009)'; MD-6 fixed basis includes only SOC2/pen-test

challenge: The $50k base price has no comparator. The anchor cited (Ren's ~$50k program set-up) is a full implementation price, not an assessment price. target_claim_or_section: §3 items 4-5: local structural profile plus synthetic rehearsal 'exercises adapter, mapping and reconciliation end to end and yields a readiness report' with no data leaving the sponsor
challenge: Synthetic data generated from a schema and k-suppressed marginals can only reproduce defects you already modelled. Conversion cost is driven by joint, record-level defects: duplicate persons, orphaned grants, misapplied contributions, free-text restrictions, successor errors. Marginal distributions hide all of these. A synthetic rehearsal will tie out by construction, so it shows only that the adapter parses the layout. Calling its output a 'readiness report' invites false GREENs in exactly the area (data quality) that 20 says moves cost 1.5-2x.

target_claim_or_section: T1 profiler 'run by the sponsor' on its desktop under NDA only; 'no personal data leaves'
challenge: The tool is a vendor-supplied executable that ingests donor PII, run before any contract exists. Sponsor IT and security (often outsourced at small foundations) will require a vendor security review or questionnaire before installation. Many will refuse it outright. The T1 output also contains control totals per fund bucket and date ranges. For sparse, high-value DAF books, k=10 on contributor count does not stop a single large fund's balance from being singled out. 13 itself makes this point about amounts as quasi-identifiers. Saying 'NDA only' understates both the security-review and privacy friction.

proposed_change: Add a T1 variant that needs no installation (spreadsheet or template reports that the sponsor fills in). Apply dominance (p%) suppression to monetary cells as well as k-count. Budget a 2-6 week sponsor security review into the pre-contract timeline. Measure the share of prospects that refuse.
disposition_rationale: Pre-contract work is not NDA-only; privacy duties
resulting_change: T0 no-install tier; T1 after IT approval; T2+ under MSA+DPA+WISP; 08, 16

target_claim_or_section: XRI-013 / 08 §4: 'second migration from same source costs far less'; adapters per named incumbent report are reusable
challenge: Reuse assumes stable report layouts. Hosted incumbents ship report and UI changes on their own release cadence and owe the sponsor no notice. Gusto's parsers carry 'beta' labels and break on masked fields. NPact is consolidating FIMS and DonorCentral, which is precisely the kind of vendor change that rewrites report layouts. The prospect pipeline is sparse: about 4 customers a year, and 1 of 26 national sponsors left Ren in 2023-26. Between two migrations from the same source, the report version may well change, and adapter maintenance per source per release is unbudgeted. In core banking, reuse works because the deconversion file is a stable vendor-supplied format, not a UI report.

Do not claim the second-migration discount until two migrations from the same source and report version have been measured. Track elapsed time between same-source deals.
disposition_rationale: Adapter drift; reports lack history detail
resulting_change: Versioned adapters; balance-level only without contracted export; 08

target_claim_or_section: Gusto-style adapters 'work without incumbent cooperation' because they consume reports the sponsor can already download
challenge: Self-service standard reports are summaries designed for operations: fund balances, statements, grant listings over a date range. They rarely carry immutable transaction IDs, reversal and void chains, fee accrual detail, unit history, or audit trails, all of which full-history per-fund reconciliation needs. NPact makes a full export a paid Professional Service and deletes data 10 business days after hosting ends. Ren gives 15 days' access. The cooperation-free path therefore yields roughly BalancesOnly plus listings. Full history, the main promise of HYP-003, still depends on the incumbent's paid, unscheduled PS export.

Make full history conditional on a contracted incumbent export, and schedule a contractual export request at notice date. Put 'incumbent export not delivered' on the exclusions list for any outcome commitment.
disposition_rationale: Adapter drift; reports lack history detail
resulting_change: Versioned adapters; balance-level only without contracted export; 08

target_claim_or_section: Rehearsals $8k-$20k total (3 runs, 40 h each at 1k scale; $20k at 1M accounts); time to production assumes 3 rehearsals x 2 weeks
challenge: In practice each mock conversion includes a fresh extract, the load, a full reconciliation, triage of every break, sponsor controller review and sign-off, and fixes to rerun. On a 1M-account, roughly 95M-transaction book a single mock is weeks of multi-person work, not under $7k. The rehearsals also depend on the extract: where only one paid extract is affordable (15 §1a), mocks 2-3 reuse stale data, and the final delta extract taken at cutover is never rehearsed. Three rehearsals is optimistic for a first-of-source conversion: practitioner guidance is 'at least two', and failed mocks add more.
evidence: 20 R5 onb_rehearsals $7,854 (1k) to $20k (1M); 20 ADVB-05 row '3 runs, 40 h each at 1k scale'; 15 §1a single-extract path; trackD row on mocks ('at least two'; Vibrant 2 mocks; reconversion mocks Sep and Nov).
proposed_change: Scale rehearsal cost with volume and exception count, not as a near-fixed line. Include the cost of each paid incumbent extract per mock. Add a mandatory delta-extract rehearsal. Model 3-5 mocks for a first-of-source conversion, and add a probability that a failed mock slips go-live past the contract end.
disposition_rationale: Rehearsal cost, freeze dependency, liability and sponsor effort understated
resulting_change: Process SLAs only, capped; freeze conditional; costs scale; 08

target_claim_or_section: Freeze ≤3 business days (target 2) and Unbound-side commitment
challenge: The final cutover extract has to come from the incumbent inside the freeze. When export is a paid PS order with no SLA, a 2-3 day freeze needs the incumbent to deliver a final extract on a set date and day. Nothing obliges it to do so, and core-conversion practice treats alignment of deconversion dates with the incumbent as a critical dependency. A 1M-account full-history load plus 100% per-fund tie-out and sign-off within 48-72 hours is also untested here. If the extract slips, either the freeze extends, breaching the public promise, or the cutover moves past the incumbent's data-deletion date.
evidence: 17 parameter table: freeze max 3 business days; 13 §2a NPact 10-business-day deletion and Ren 15-day access; CUInsight: aligning deconversion and data-file delivery dates with the new provider is critical; American Banker: uncertainty over how quickly the incumbent delivers deconversion programs.
proposed_change: Make the freeze target conditional on an incumbent extract SLA, or on a sponsor-controlled direct database extract. Publish the freeze as 'N business days after receipt of a conforming final extract'. Negotiate post-termination access extensions in the Extraction Plan, and rehearse the timed final extract.
disposition_rationale: Rehearsal cost, freeze dependency, liability and sponsor effort understated
resulting_change: Process SLAs only, capped; freeze conditional; costs scale; 08

target_claim_or_section: XRI-011 published migration SLA and outcome commitments (maturity level 4); 16 §5 'measured freeze ... published exit price'
challenge: A pre-revenue startup that publishes outcome commitments on full-history fund-level reconciliation is taking on uncapped liability against inputs it does not control: incumbent extracts, sponsor cleansing, and the sponsor's own decisions. Stripe can offer a 10-day SLA because its exclusions are narrow and it has a balance sheet. Unbound has $0.7-1.2M at G1. One failed migration of a donor-facing financial book (FFTC's $654.5k abandoned implementation) would consume the reserve and the reference base. Exclude incumbent and sponsor dependencies. Get an E&O insurance quote before publishing. Defer outcome commitments until level-4 metrics exist from ≥3 measured migrations.
disposition_rationale: Rehearsal cost, freeze dependency, liability and sponsor effort understated
resulting_change: Process SLAs only, capped; freeze conditional; costs scale; 08

target_claim_or_section: §5 maturity model levels 0-5; 'claim a level only from measured data'; XRI-009 adopts it as Transitus targets
challenge: The levels mix binary practices (≥2 mocks, published exclusions) with thresholds that have no stated measurement protocol or denominator: '>50% of migrations need no engineering change', 'exceptions per 1k', 'post-go-live defects per 1k funds'. At 2-4 migrations a year, a percentage such as >50% takes years to mean anything, and no incumbent reports enough to be placed on the scale (CLM-020). Exemplars are assigned by anecdote, for example 'typical CU core conversion' = level 1 and 'many FIMS replacements' = level 0. The model cannot be used comparatively, and it only becomes self-assessable after many measured runs.

resulting_change: Definitions and minimum n required; exemplars illustrative; 08

target_claim_or_section: Sponsor hours 584 (1k) to 934 (10k) to 9,016 (1M); sponsor cleansing as 'data clean-up' line; history gaps 'documented, not invented'

Peak load also collides with year-end, because contract ends cluster at fiscal or calendar year. Add an explicit history-reconstruction cost line, or a 'HistoryIncomplete accepted' decision with donor-communication cost. Validate against ≥3 sponsor timesheets (CNV-EVB-002).
disposition_rationale: Rehearsal cost, freeze dependency, liability and sponsor effort understated
resulting_change: Process SLAs only, capped; freeze conditional; costs scale; 08

target_claim_or_section: §3 'lowest defensible capital for a self-sustaining business is about $4-5M' (ER-7 P50 $5.06M; P10 $4.03M)
challenge: The headline is the P10-P50 band of a route whose partner existence is unverified. P90 is $6.78M, the adverse case is a $11.4M floor that never turns positive, and the Monte Carlo does not price the chance that no partner exists. Rerunning Routes.fs to 180 months gives an ER-7 adverse deficit of $22.6M, still not cash-positive. An investor would read '$4-5M' as the raise size, but it is the optimistic half of a distribution that is itself conditional on a partner existing.

target_claim_or_section: §12 MC P10/P50/P90 capital percentiles for all routes
challenge: The percentiles mix full capital figures with draws truncated at 60 months: 12.7% of ER-7 draws, 18% of ER-4, 61% of ER-6 and 99.7% of ER-2 are 60-month deficits, not totals. A percentile over right-censored values is biased low, and the bias is largest in the upper tail (P90) that an investor uses to size reserves. For ER-2 the 'capital' P50 of $1.80M is just 60 months of burn.

resulting_change: Routes: 8% churn, go-live lag, 120-month horizon, payback month; ER-2 reported as never self-funding; 15

target_claim_or_section: §2 ER-2 (and ER-1/ER-3/ER-6 base) reported in the 'Capital' column

It can never be cash-positive at any horizon, so its 'capital' of $1.87M is purely a function of the 60-month horizon. resulting_change: Routes: 8% churn, go-live lag, 120-month horizon, payback month; ER-2 reported as never self-funding; 15

Cumulative cash at month 60 is still -$4.1M, and cumulative payback comes in month 89. ER-4 direct pays back in month 99. target_claim_or_section: §4 revenue potential: '10k-account sponsor worth $0.8-1.5M a year'; ER-7 basis '3-10k-account sponsors' at $300k each
challenge: $300k net to vendor at $81 x 0.7 implies about 5.3k accounts per customer, so ER-7 base needs about 60k licensed accounts from 11 sponsors by month 60 (about 41 by month 180). Sponsors with 3-10k accounts sit mostly in SEG-001 (82 national sponsors), which the package itself calls least mobile (1 of 26 left). The serviceable pool of 3-10k-account licensees is probably a few dozen, so the model assumes a large share capture.

resulting_change: Stated; population cap not modelled; gap recorded

challenge: The package's own evidence undercuts the channel route. Administrators acquire rather than license (SEG-013). The only distributor precedent (SEI) already chose TIFIN. target_claim_or_section: §2 staged G0-G1-G2 cumulative capital ('~$5M P50 (ER-7)' at G2)
challenge: The staged totals are not additive in the model. ER-7 is simulated standalone from month 0, with its own $1.6M build and 15 months to revenue. target_claim_or_section: G1 exit '≥2 paying customers' and the evidence-first wedge as basis for the next round
challenge: G1 success means about $30-120k ARR from copyable services. target_claim_or_section: §12 route model structure (Routes.fs)

target_claim_or_section: §5 positioning hypotheses 1-3 (verifiable migration, replayable vetting, licence-not-capture)

target_claim_or_section: V-1 win/loss interviews (sample = 10 sponsors that switched or evaluated)

target_claim_or_section: §2 'integrated platform' as the observed, stated switch trigger (Vermont, CNY, Arizona)

Those are after-the-fact explanations written to justify a disruption to donors, not procurement criteria. 24 of the 44 switch rows say 'not stated'. The real reasons at most CFs are mundane: the vendor sunset or forced a re-host, a new CEO or CFO arrived, the auditor flagged reconciliation, or peers at a CF conference recommended Foundant. Calling integration 'VERIFIED' overstates what a donor notice can establish.

target_claim_or_section: §1-§2 switching cost framed mainly as data-migration risk
challenge: The package treats switching cost as a data problem (mapping, reconciliation, freeze days). For me most of the cost is people and institutions. My staff need 6-12 months to reach proficiency on a new system. I lose year-end giving season, so the window is really Feb-Sep. Every advisor and donor login, saved recurring grant and report has to be re-learned. The finance committee and board have to approve. My auditor has to re-test controls on a new system, which means first-year audit fee uplift and a SOC 1 reliance gap. Insurance and cyber questionnaires get redone. None of this is reduced by a Merkle-sealed staging area. The sponsors in the switch log tolerated 2-9 week freezes, which suggests the data piece is not the binding constraint.

target_claim_or_section: §2-§3 entrant viability (G1-G2 capital $0.7-5M; no SOC history)

Specify mitigants buyers would credit: partner or parent balance sheet, a hosted-data transition-services clause, a funded runway disclosure and a named fallback operator. Note that licence-via-channel (G2) partly fixes this only if the channel partner carries the risk.

target_claim_or_section: §3 minimum viable entry point = a PAID migration assessment
challenge: I would not pay for an assessment of a migration I have not decided to do, especially when every vendor I would actually choose will scope my conversion for free during the sales cycle. Foundant documents a standard migration-site validation process as part of implementation, and the package itself says free migration is table stakes in nonprofit CRM. 08 §6 also contradicts 16 §3: 08 prices T0-T1 free and T2-T3 paid, while 16 calls the paid assessment the minimum viable commercial entry and sets the G1 exit at ≥2 paying customers. A paid T2-T3 needs a DPA and real data, which a satisfied sponsor will not hand to an unproven vendor before deciding to leave.

proposed_change: Reconcile 08 and 16: make the assessment free (T0-T1) and treat paid T2-T3 as an implementation deposit for sponsors that have already decided to switch. Remove the 'paid assessment' wedge as a revenue claim and count its cost as CAC.

target_claim_or_section: §3 'contract-end back-schedule' and 16/22 V-5 'contract-end windows' (≥10 windows in 24 months)
challenge: A contract end is not a window for a satisfied customer. Most of my vendor agreements auto-renew, and the notice date is the point where I use a competitor quote to renegotiate price, not to leave. An entrant that turns up at my notice date mostly becomes free leverage for my incumbent. V-5 counts windows from 990 payments and DNS, which shows when a contract could end but not whether the buyer is in-market. 06 §4 names auto-renewal as a lock-in mechanic yet the strategy still treats the calendar as pipeline. Real windows are the forced ones (sunset, divestiture, re-host), and the log shows the incumbent or Foundant is already positioned when those happen.

resulting_change: V-5 pass rule requires active evaluations; 22

target_claim_or_section: §3 W02/W03/W20, W01, W25 and §2 donor row (freeze, history, grant delays as opportunities)
challenge: The research catalogues donor and charity pain (freezes, re-registration, truncated history, slow grants) and then concedes in 07 §4 that this pain does not change purchasing. The matrix still lists these as places 'Unbound can solve', and they reappear as positioning line 1. As the buyer, donor complaints reach me as a handful of service tickets. resulting_change: Positioning ranked below scope; price/exit as hygiene; 07, 16

My counsel will want transition services and data return clauses, which the incumbent will match the moment I ask; the package rates replication as 'Trivial'. A differentiator the incumbent can copy in a renewal redline is a negotiating chip for me, not a reason to switch.

target_claim_or_section: §1 G0 total and 16 §2 G0 capital

target_claim_or_section: minutesPerTouch: exceptionNoAi = nativeD / f; doc 10 §6 'at pessimistic 0.9 the AI step is worth about $4'
challenge: The AI factor is applied backwards. Native (MD-5) minutes are fixed inputs taken from the activity register's AI-native column, and the no-AI counterfactual (MD-4) is derived as native/f. Lowering AI efficacy therefore makes MD-4 cheaper and leaves MD-5 unchanged: the AI-native mode's own cost and break-even cannot respond to the AI evidence. The '~10% from AI' and '$4 at 0.9' figures re-label savings and do not stress-test them. ai_assist_duration_factor is not in the MD-5 tornado at all.

If native minutes are scaled honestly (duration_mult_native=f/0.6): f=0.88 gives MD-5 38.1 min, $98 variable, $1.51B break-even (P50 $1.77B); f=0.97 gives 42.0 min, $102 variable, $1.53B, and the AI step is about -$0.2/acct.
proposed_change: Anchor the MD-4 (no-AI) minutes as inputs and derive MD-5 = MD-4 × f, so the AI factor flows into MD-5 cost, the tornado and the Monte Carlo. Restate CLM-011 as conditional on f.

resulting_change: Exception minutes now inputs; AI-native = exception x factor; test added; 09, 10

target_claim_or_section: §6 and PAR-007: AI cuts minutes per touch by 40% (0.6; range 0.4-0.9)
challenge: The base 0.6 equals the most favourable lab result (Noy & Zhang 2023: about 40% time saved on short, stylized writing tasks) and better than BCG's inside-frontier result (Dell'Acqua et al. 2023: 25% faster). Field evidence is much smaller. In customer support, Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond find about 14% more resolutions per hour (f≈0.88), concentrated among novices, with little gain for experienced agents. The residual exceptions here are worked by compliance and accounting specialists, exactly where those gains vanish. Humlum & Vestergaard's Danish administrative data show about 3% of work hours saved and precise-zero earnings and hours effects. The low end of 0.4 has no empirical support.
evidence: Literature as cited. f=0.88 (honest propagation): AI step $4.1/acct instead of $17.5; MD-5 human minutes 26→38 (+47%).
proposed_change: Set base f to 0.85-0.9 and range to 0.75-1.0. Treat 0.6 as an upside case to be shown by the V-7 time study (OQ-011).
disposition_rationale: 0.6 is a lab result; field evidence smaller

target_claim_or_section: EV-E08, EV-E10, EV-E04, EV-E13 native touch probabilities and prevention efficacies
challenge: Prevention appears to be double counted. EV-E08's native touch rate (0.0117) is already based on 'change-driven vetting central estimate ~5 reviews per 1000 grants', and the same change-driven monitoring is then applied again as prevention (efficacy 0.5). EV-E10's native touch rate of 0.09 is calibrated to a replay proxy (7.4-11.2% routed) that presumably already applies policy rules, and 'pre-validated policy rules' then remove another 40%. EV-E13 and EV-E04 follow the same pattern. So the $33.5 'prevention' step is partly a second application of the redesign already priced into the native touch rates.
evidence: Scratch rerun with prevention zeroed for E08/E10/E13 and E04 cut 0.6→0.3: MD-5 rises 26.0→36.2 min and $85→$101 variable; break-even $1.46B→$1.53B (P50 $1.74B→$1.81B); the prevention step falls from $33.5 to $9.9.
proposed_change: For each event, state whether the native-touch basis is measured before or after the prevention mechanism. Apply prevention only to pre-mechanism rates.
disposition_rationale: Prevention double counted for vetting and reconciliation
resulting_change: E08/E13 native touch rebased to pre-prevention; E10 efficacy 0.4->0.25; 09, 10

target_claim_or_section: §3 decomposition: deterministic workflow $102 (MD-1→MD-3) vs AI ~10%
challenge: The 'deterministic workflow' step takes MD-3's structured-event touch rates directly from the AI-native activity column (E03 0.60→0.03; E08 0.37→0.0117; E13 0.05→0.01; E20 0.016→0.0009). Nothing shows these rates come from rules and not from AI classification or extraction, such as check and remittance parsing or purpose matching. The 97% straight-through rate assumed for contribution posting covers checks and securities. Ops benchmarks for mature payment and securities processing only approach that level after years of tuning; it is not an entry-year rate. The decomposition is order-dependent and fragile. With touch rates ×1.5 and durations ×1.3, the 'exception-only design' step turns negative (-$20/acct), because MD-4's derived minutes (native/0.6, e.g. E10 42 min vs 12.4 conventional) exceed the conventional ones.
evidence: events.csv basis column cites ACT ai_native values. Tornado touch_mult_native=2 → $1.56B. Scratch rerun touch×1.5 and duration×1.3: MD-5 48.7 min, $111 variable, $1.56B; decomposition MD-3→MD-4 = -$20.2.
proposed_change: Label MD-3 touch rates as unmeasured ramp-year targets. Use an entry-year touch multiplier of 1.5-2.0 that falls with volume (learning curve). Report Shapley-averaged attribution over step orderings, not one sequential path.
disposition_rationale: MD-3 touch rates are AI-native targets
resulting_change: Labelled as unmeasured targets; covered by touch range and stress

target_claim_or_section: MD-5 fixed = MD-4 + ~$0.1M 'AI evaluation and governance'
challenge: Induced work from AI is underpriced. $0.1M does not cover model risk management of the kind regulators expect for automated eligibility decisions (SR 11-7-style independent validation, evaluation-set maintenance, drift monitoring, change control when vendor models are deprecated, and audit of AI decisions), plus the human QA sampling of auto-cleared items. Humlum & Vestergaard report that AI creates new tasks, including checking AI output, for a material share of workers. At base, the AI step saves $17.5/acct against $100k of fixed cost, so it pays only above about 5.7k accounts. That is roughly the base break-even scale ($1.46B / $250k ≈ 5.8k accounts), so the AI step is about break-even at entry.
evidence: Scratch rerun with +$0.3M on AI modes (MD-5 2.6M; MD-6 1.9M; MD-7 2.25M): MD-5 break-even $1.46B→$1.65B (P50 $1.82B); MD-6 $0.85B→$1.01B. At f=0.88 the AI step ($4.1/acct) needs about 24k accounts to cover even $0.1M.
proposed_change: Add an explicit AI-oversight line: 0.5-1 FTE model risk management plus validation, evals and QA sampling, $250-400k. Add a 2-5% QA sample of auto-cleared compliance events as touched minutes.
disposition_rationale: AI oversight underpriced
resulting_change: +$0.1-0.2M fixed for AI oversight and model-risk management; 10

target_claim_or_section: EV-E21/E22 sponsor_min_native (audit 7200→3600; reporting 4800→2640)
challenge: Audit preparation is assumed to halve in AI-native mode. Automating eligibility and approval decisions widens audit scope instead (ITGC and automated-control testing, SOC 1 Type II on the decision logic, evidence of model change management), so audit minutes are more likely to stay flat or rise. The halving is ASSUMPTION ('evidence-by-default controls') with no auditor input.
evidence: Scratch rerun audit native = 7200 and reporting = 4200: MD-5 break-even $1.46B→$1.49B (P50 $1.77B).
proposed_change: Hold audit preparation at conventional minutes until an auditor walkthrough (OQ-004) supports a reduction. Add AI-decision audit scope to E22.
disposition_rationale: Audit scope widens with automation
resulting_change: E22 held at conventional minutes; 09

target_claim_or_section: PAR-020 activity_mult applied identically to all modes; no rebound
challenge: There is no rebound (Jevons) effect. Revenue is in bps of assets, but the model's own design lowers per-grant friction (instant grants, closed picker, self-service), which invites more and smaller grants and more contacts per dollar of assets; frictionless platforms market exactly that behaviour. Costs scale with event counts and revenue does not. The model holds frequency equal across modes, so the AI-native mode never pays for the demand its lower prices create.
evidence: Scratch rerun activity_mult 1.3 (MD-5 only relevant; MD-1 held at 1.0): MD-5 26→33.8 min, $85→$103 variable, break-even $1.46B→$1.53B, against MD-1 at $2.11B.
proposed_change: Add a mode-specific activity elasticity (grants per $ of assets +15-40% in AI-native/self-service modes) and report break-even per grant as well as per asset.
disposition_rationale: Rebound effect
resulting_change: Covered by activity range (0.6-2.06); no mode-specific elasticity

target_claim_or_section: PAR-009 fail_mult_automated base 0.8 (automation reduces failures)
challenge: The base case assumes automated modes fail 20% less often. Dell'Acqua et al. found AI-assisted workers were 19 percentage points less likely to be correct on tasks outside the frontier, and over-reliance on automation leads to errors that propagate. In AI-native mode, the cases that reach a person are by construction the out-of-frontier ones, so a failure multiplier of at least 1.0 is the neutral prior. Failures are already about 19% of MD-5 event cost (doc 09 §5).
evidence: Scratch rerun fail_mult_automated 1.2: MD-5 variable $85→$90; break-even $1.46B→$1.48B.
proposed_change: Set the base to 1.0 with a range of 0.7-1.5, and correlate it with the touch and duration multipliers in the Monte Carlo.
disposition_rationale: No evidence automation lowers failure rates
resulting_change: fail_mult_automated base 1.0 (0.7-1.5); systemic failures recorded as risk

target_claim_or_section: §4 Monte Carlo: 'independent parameters (ASSUMPTION)'
challenge: Productivity parameters are drawn independently, so the tails are too narrow. Harder residual cases, higher touch rates, longer durations, a weaker AI factor and higher failure rates share a common cause (task difficulty and immature processes), and in the field evidence they move together. Independent triangular draws cancel out, so P90 for MD-5 at 20 bps ($2.21B) understates the downside. A correlated pessimistic case lands at the conventional break-even.
evidence: Preferred combined case (f 0.88 propagated, durations ×1.15 for harder residuals, touch ×1.5, prevention double-count removed, fail_mult 1.0, +$0.3M AI governance, audit not halved): MD-5 88.9 min/acct-yr (vs 26), $165 variable (vs $85), break-even $2.07B (P50 $2.05B) vs MD-1 $2.11B (P50 $2.44B); MD-4 without AI $1.88B beats MD-5. MD-6 rises only $0.85B→$1.01B.
proposed_change: Introduce a shared 'process maturity' latent factor (rank correlation 0.5-0.7) across touch, duration, AI-factor and failure draws. Report the correlated P90 and the break-even at which MD-5 equals MD-1.
disposition_rationale: Independent draws understated tails
resulting_change: Correlated Monte Carlo (rho 0.5) for modes and routes; correlated stress scenario; 10, 15

target_claim_or_section: Answer 1 and §7: 'fundamentally lower variable cost' (26 min vs 183)
challenge: Time saved is treated as cost saved. Minutes are priced at a loaded hourly rate, as if labour were perfectly divisible. At entry scale (about 6k accounts), 26 min/acct is about 2.6k hours a year, spread across ops, compliance, accounting and controller roles with separation-of-duties and coverage requirements. Integer staffing makes the true marginal saving much lower than the minutes imply. This is the productivity-paradox mechanism: Humlum & Vestergaard find time savings were not converted into hours or wage changes, and the Brynjolfsson-Rock-Syverson J-curve predicts that unmeasured complementary investment (process redesign, training) arrives before measured gains.
evidence: Base MD-5 at 5.8k accounts: 26 min × 5.8k ≈ 2.5k h ≈ 1.4 FTE across 4 expertise pools; the preferred case is about 8.6k h ≈ 4.8 FTE. Fixed-cost sensitivity dominates the tornado.
proposed_change: Model staffed FTE as step functions by expertise pool (ceil(hours/1,600) with a 0.5 FTE floor per pool), and add a 12-24 month ramp with elevated touch rates (J-curve) to the capital model in doc 15.
disposition_rationale: FTE step functions
resulting_change: Utilisation factor added; step functions by pool deferred

target_claim_or_section: §5 lowest defensible cost $90-120k; steward sized by workload with 0.25 FTE floor; ≤45 min exceptions with 20-30% auto-resolution
challenge: The registry floor relies on the same minutes-to-dollars conversion and unmeasured exception parameters. Cheaper vetting is also likely to broaden the grantee mix: sponsors admit more fiscal sponsors, churches, international and equivalency cases, and their exceptions run well above 45 minutes. The 0.25 FTE accountable owner also has to supervise automated evidence collection. RA-2 already shows that automation raises cost through connector maintenance, which is direct evidence of induced work, and the same logic applies to monitoring false positives.
evidence: Doc 05 §2 RA-2: human hours −30% but cost +$35k versus RA-1. Doc 05 §3: the human-hour line doubles at an 8% change rate. No measured exception minutes (doc 21 gap 5).
proposed_change: Present $90-120k as a floor conditional on V-3/V-7 measurements. Add a grantee-mix elasticity and a steward floor of 0.5 FTE in the central case.
disposition_rationale: Registry floor conditional on measurement
resulting_change: Stated as conditional on V-3/V-7; 05
